data.title: [FEATURE REQUEST] Enable returning metadata-only from keys backed by the Zenoh storage manager plugin
data.body:
# Context
When using Zenoh storages (e.g., rocksdb, filesystem, s3) for large binary payloads (images, point clouds, etc.), it is useful to look at the metadata of the value before requesting the full payload (checking for freshness, enforcing high consistency).

Currently, any `get` query to a storage returns the full `Sample` containing the complete payload. There is no way to probe key existence, payload size, or HLC timestamp without transferring the entire payload over the network.

# Current Workarounds / Alternatives
The absence of a first-class metadata query forces users into suboptimal workarounds:
- Dual Key-Space: Creating `<key>/data` and `<key>/meta` parallel keys makes it hard to keep them in sync
- Client-side Truncation: Slicing the payload client-side does not save network bandwidth since the payload is already transmitted over the wire.

# Proposed Feature
Add a standardized, reserved query selector parameter (e.g., `_meta_only=true`) to `zenoh-plugin-storage-manager` that strips the payload but returns associated metadata.

Query Syntax: `my/storage/key?_meta_only=true`

Expected Reply:
- payload: `ZBytes::empty()` (0 payload bytes transferred)
- timestamp: Preserved from the stored `Sample` (HLC)
- attachment: An attachment carrying metadata:
  - `payload_len`: The original size of the payload in bytes
  - `original_attachment`: The original sample attachment (if any)

Maybe this could be done in phases:
1. Handle the parameter directly inside `zenoh-plugin-storage-manager` before querying backends, or intercept the backend's response and strip the payload before wire serialization. This ensures compatibility across all backends.
2. Find a fast path per individual backend (?)

data.title: With Rust 1.75 fix dependency to static_init 1.0.3
data.body:
## Description

On Linux, when building zenoh in debug mode with Rust 1.75 and `zenoh-pinned-deps-1-75` dependency it fails.

To reproduce:
`cargo check --manifest-path ci/zenoh-1-75/Cargo.toml`

Result:
```log
error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate `parking_lot` in this scope
   --> /home/ubuntu/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/static_init-1.0.3/src/lazy_sequentializer.rs:336:13
    |
336 |         use parking_lot::lock_api::GetThreadId;
    |             ^^^^^^^^^^^ use of unresolved module or unlinked crate `parking_lot`
    |
    = help: if you wanted to use a crate named `parking_lot`, use `cargo add parking_lot` to add it to your `Cargo.toml`

error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate `parking_lot` in this scope
   --> /home/ubuntu/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/static_init-1.0.3/src/lazy_sequentializer.rs:371:21
    |
371 |                 use parking_lot::lock_api::GetThreadId;
    |                     ^^^^^^^^^^^ use of unresolved module or unlinked crate `parking_lot`
    |
    = help: if you wanted to use a crate named `parking_lot`, use `cargo add parking_lot` to add it to your `Cargo.toml`

error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate `parking_lot` in this scope
   --> /home/ubuntu/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/static_init-1.0.3/src/lazy_sequentializer.rs:338:13
    |
338 |             parking_lot::RawThreadId.nonzero_thread_id().into(),
    |             ^^^^^^^^^^^ use of unresolved module or unlinked crate `parking_lot`
    |
    = help: if you wanted to use a crate named `parking_lot`, use `cargo add parking_lot` to add it to your `Cargo.toml`

error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate `parking_lot` in this scope
   --> /home/ubuntu/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/static_init-1.0.3/src/lazy_sequentializer.rs:372:26
    |
372 |                 if id == parking_lot::RawThreadId.nonzero_thread_id().into() {
    |                          ^^^^^^^^^^^ use of unresolved module or unlinked crate `parking_lot`
    |
    = help: if you wanted to use a crate named `parking_lot`, use `cargo add parking_lot` to add it to your `Cargo.toml`
```

The issue is in `static_init` 1.0.3:
on Linux the dependency to `parking_lot` depends on a `debug_mode` config which is not activated when `debug_assertions` is set (i.e. build in debug).

It has been [fixed in 1.0.4](https://gitlab.com/okannen/static_init/-/commit/7b6aeb0f363df4ad39fd7c69d875372285d7f0d8#line_ba2f135ee_A6), but it required Rust >= 1.82.

### What does this PR do?

The fix here is to depend on `static_init` 1.0.3 with the feature `"debug_order"`. This forces the `debug_mode` config and hence the dependency to `parking_lot`.

data.title: fix: stop calling user code under runtime/session locks
data.body:
## Summary

`cancel_query`, `cancel_liveliness_query`, the liveliness-query reply path, and `RuntimeTransportEventHandler::new_unicast`/`new_multicast` all held a write guard (`self.0.state` or `transport_handlers`) across a call into user code — a callback invocation, or a `Callback`'s `Drop` (which can run a user-supplied hook). A callback that re-enters and takes the same lock self-deadlocks: one thread, no race, every time.

Also adds [`lock-tripwire`](https://github.com/YuanYuYuan/lock-tripwire), an opt-in, debug-time tripwire that asserts no tracked lock is held at the one call-out site this fix couldn't remove structurally (the liveliness-query reply), so a regression of this shape fails fast and by name instead of hanging.

## The fix

Each site now either scopes the guard to the `remove()`/`clone()` call alone, or clones the callback and drops the guard before calling it — matching the pattern this file's own `undeclare_querier_inner` already uses:

```rust
// before
let mut state = zwrite!(self.0.state);
match state.liveliness_queries.remove(&qid) { ... }   // guard live across the Drop of the removed value

// after
let removed = zwrite!(self.0.state).liveliness_queries.remove(&qid);
match removed { ... }   // guard released at the end of the statement
```

`new_unicast`/`new_multicast` collect the registered handlers (cheap `Arc` clones) before releasing `transport_handlers`, then call each outside the lock.

## Test coverage: disclosed, not fabricated

No dedicated failing-baseline test accompanies this fix, for the same reason #2744 in this repo states for its own commits 3–5: each of these closes a race that needs a callback to land inside a window bounded by one guard release and the next acquisition. A test that hit the window would be timing-dependent; one that missed it would read as proof of absence. The argument for each site is the control flow, stated at the code — matching this repository's own precedent for exactly this class of fix.

The one site with a genuinely stable, always-reachable assertion (not a timing-dependent hang) is the liveliness-query reply path, which now asserts under `--features reentrancy-tripwire`. The other three restructurings remove a lock-held-across-call-out shape that reappears identically at four sites in this same file's `undeclare_querier_inner` — the same defect family, already fixed there.

## Overlap with YuanYuYuan/zenoh#1 (lock-tripwire on top of #2744)

This PR introduces the same `commons/zenoh-core` tracking plumbing as [YuanYuYuan/zenoh#1](https://github.com/YuanYuYuan/zenoh/pull/1), independently, because this fix has nothing to do with `AdvancedSubscriber` and shouldn't depend on #2744 merging first. Whichever of the two lands first should absorb the other's infra commits on rebase — flagging this now so a reviewer isn't surprised by the duplication.

## Before and after

| | today | with this change |
|---|---|---|
| `cancel_query`/`cancel_liveliness_query` | guard held across the removed value's `Drop` | guard released at the `remove()` statement |
| liveliness-query reply | guard held across `callback.call(reply)` | callback cloned, guard dropped, then called — asserted under `reentrancy-tripwire` |
| `new_unicast`/`new_multicast` | `transport_handlers` held across each handler call | handlers collected, lock released, then called |
| a callback that re-enters any of the above | deadlocks | proceeds normally |

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --locked --all-features`: clean.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --locked --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
- `cargo fmt --check`: clean.
- `cargo test -p zenoh --lib --features unstable`: 40 tests pass, including the `link_weights`/`interceptor_cache` suites (the ones a prior wiring attempt at one of these sites broke, so specifically checked).

## Breaking changes

None. `reentrancy-tripwire` is opt-in and off by default.

data.title: router silently stops accepting all new connections after restart (all threads idle-parked, no crash, no log)
data.body:
## Describe the bug

Under a fairly aggressive restart/reconnect stress cycle, a `zenohd` router
(mode `router`, usrpwd + ACL enabled, one REST + one storage_manager plugin)
occasionally (~1 in 5 restarts in our testing) reaches a state where it stops
accepting **any** new connection — both its own unicast transport listener
(`udp/...?rel=1`) and the co-located REST plugin's HTTP listener on
`127.0.0.1:8000`.

- The process stays alive, uses ~0% CPU, and never panics or logs anything
  after the normal startup sequence (last line logged is
  `Zenoh can be reached at: udp/x.x.x.x:7447?rel=1`).
- `netstat` inside the container shows both listeners still in `LISTEN`
  state, with a non-zero `Recv-Q` on the REST TCP listener (connections are
  reaching the kernel backlog but nothing ever calls `accept()`).
- Existing already-established sessions (if any) keep working; only *new*
  connection attempts are affected.
- Restarting the router process is the only way to recover.

We attached `gdb` (via a debug sidecar container sharing the router's PID
namespace, since the router's own container has no `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`) and
took `thread apply all bt` for all 18 threads while the router was in this
state. Every single thread — including the one named `acc-0` (the
`ZRuntime::Acceptor` pool worker) — was parked in the ordinary tokio idle
path:

```
<tokio::runtime::io::driver::Driver>::turn ()
<tokio::runtime::time::Driver>::park_internal ()
<tokio::runtime::scheduler::multi_thread::worker::Context>::park_internal ()
tokio::runtime::scheduler::multi_thread::worker::run ()
```

i.e. **this is not a classic mutex deadlock** — no thread is spinning or
blocked mid-critical-section. The Acceptor runtime genuinely has nothing
scheduled, which combined with new connections queuing unhandled in the
kernel backlog suggests the accept-side bookkeeping got into a state where
new links are being rejected (or simply never dispatched) without any work
ever reaching the Acceptor pool again.

Looking at `zenoh-transport-1.10.1/src/unicast/manager.rs`,
`TransportManager::handle_new_link_unicast` gates new links behind an
`AtomicUsize` counter (`state.unicast.incoming`) checked against
`config.unicast.accept_pending` (default 100):

```rust
if incoming_counter.load(SeqCst) >= self.config.unicast.accept_pending {
    // logs at tracing::trace! only, then closes the link and returns
    let _ = link.close().await;
    return;
}
...
incoming_counter.fetch_add(1, SeqCst);
self.task_controller.spawn_with_rt(zenoh_runtime::ZRuntime::Acceptor, async move {
    if tokio::time::timeout(accept_timeout, accept_link(link, &c_manager)).await.is_err() {
        tracing::debug!(...);
    }
    incoming_counter.fetch_sub(1, SeqCst); // only reached if the spawned future ever completes
});
```

If the spawned future for even one accepted link never resolves (so the
`fetch_sub` is never reached, and the `timeout()` racing it also never gets
polled again to fire), `incoming_counter` would leak upward and eventually
reach `accept_pending`, after which **every subsequent connection is
silently rejected** at `tracing::trace!` level (invisible at the `info`
level we run at) — which matches everything we observed, including the
Acceptor pool going idle (the fast-reject path does no lasting work) and the
total silence in the logs.

We were not able to pin down *which* code path leaves the counter
unbalanced — our build is a release/stripped binary so local-variable-level
attribution wasn't possible, and we could not yet produce a minimal,
reliably reproducible standalone repro. We're filing this as a "here's what
we found" report in case the mechanism (or the trace-level-only rejection
log, which makes this very hard to diagnose in production) rings a bell for
someone more familiar with this code path — happy to help narrow it down
further if that's useful, including sharing the full backtraces.

Separately, and possibly worth a look regardless of the above: the REST
plugin's listener being affected by the same event as the transport-unicast
listener suggests they may share more Acceptor-pool state than expected, or
the REST plugin has its own, similarly-shaped bug — we haven't looked into
its code path at all.

## To reproduce

We don't have a small, reliable, standalone repro yet — the following is
the (much larger, application-specific) sequence under which we observed it
appear intermittently (roughly 1 in 5 attempts):

1. Router config: `mode: router`, one `udp/...?rel=1` unicast listener,
   `access_control` enabled with `usrpwd`-based subjects, `rest` +
   `storage_manager` plugins loaded, one outgoing `connect` to an upstream
   router (also usrpwd + `?rel=1`).
2. Repeatedly (in a loop): restart the router process (fresh container each
   time), then rapidly connect and disconnect one or more `zenoh::open()`
   client sessions against it (each doing ~2000 `declare_subscriber` +
   `declare_queryable`/`get` calls and then dropping the session within
   ~1-2 seconds), interleaved with restarting a separate long-lived
   publisher client that also reconnects to the same router.
3. After some number of iterations, one of the fresh router instances comes
   up, logs the normal startup sequence, and then never accepts another
   connection (poll the REST endpoint or try to reconnect a client to
   detect it).

We suspect the density of connect/disconnect churn right around router
startup is what matters more than any single step above, but haven't
isolated it further.

## System info

- Zenoh version: `v1.10.1-1211779c3647f5a96713dade452c546a07823580`, `zenohd v1.10.1 built with rustc 1.97.1 (8bab26f4f 2026-07-14)`
- Distribution: `eclipse/zenoh` Docker image (Alpine Linux 3.24.1), `zenohd -c config.json5`
- Host: Docker Desktop for Windows, WSL2 backend, container run with `--network bridge` (not `--network host`)
- CPU: x86_64
- Relevant config excerpts: `access_control.enabled: true` with `usrpwd`+`zids`/`usernames`-based subjects, `transport.auth.usrpwd.dictionary_file` set on the affected router, `transport.unicast.accept_pending` left at default (100)

data.title: /etc/zenohd Gets Wiped on Every Package Upgrade
data.body:
### Describe the bug

Hi Zenoh team,

First of all, thanks for maintaining the official Debian repo — it makes installation super convenient.

I wanted to bring up a minor annoyance I've been running into on Ubuntu 26.04. I installed Zenoh from the Eclipse repository (the standard `deb https://download.eclipse.org/zenoh/debian-repo/ ...`), and I've noticed that every time I run `sudo apt update`, the `/etc/zenohd` folder gets wiped out. Not during an upgrade, not during a remove — just a plain `apt update`.

This caught me off guard because I usually keep my custom `DEFAULT_CONFIG.json5` in there, and after a routine update, it's just gone and I have to recreate it.

---

I did some digging and found the exact culprit:

I extracted the `zenohd_1.9.0_amd64.deb` and looked at the `DEBIAN/postrm` script:

```sh
case "$1" in
    purge|remove|upgrade|failed-upgrade|abort-install|abort-upgrade|disappear)
    userdel zenohd > /dev/null 2>&1 || true
    rm -rf /etc/zenohd /var/zenohd
    ;;
esac
```

The problem is that `upgrade` is included in the destructive branch. So every time the package upgrades, the *old* postrm runs with `upgrade` as the argument and **deletes `/etc/zenohd` before dpkg's conffile handling even gets a chance**. This means even though `/etc/zenohd/zenohd.json5` is correctly registered as a conffile, it gets physically wiped out before dpkg can preserve it.

Also, `/var/zenohd` (the daemon's state directory) gets nuked on every upgrade too, and the `zenohd` system user is deleted and recreated.

I'm currently on version 1.10.1 and checked the postrm — it's still using the same logic, so the issue persists in the latest release.

**It would be great if a future version could fix this by restricting the `rm -rf` to the `purge` case only.** That's the Debian Policy way — config and state removal should only happen on purge, not on upgrade or remove.

Happy to provide more details if needed. Appreciate your work on this!

Cheers

### To reproduce

**To reproduce:**

- Install an older version of `zenohd` (e.g., 1.9.0) from the Eclipse repository.
- Upgrade to a newer version (e.g., 1.10.0 or 1.10.1) via `sudo apt upgrade`.
- Check `/etc/zenohd` — the entire directory, including any custom configuration files, will be gone.
- Check `/var/zenohd` — the state directory will also be empty.

**Expected result:** Configuration files in `/etc/zenohd` should be preserved across upgrades, as per standard Debian package behavior.

**Actual result:** The directory is wiped out on every upgrade.

### System info

- Platform: Ubuntu 26.04 (amd64)
- CPU: AMD Ryzen 9950X
- Zenoh version: 1.10.1

data.title: feat: `#advertise_addr=observed` connection param
data.body:
## Description

Adds `advertise_addr=<mode>` parameter that is forwarded via Hello messages, where `observed` is the only current mode.

**NOTE**:

I take no personal credit for this feature outside of orchestrating the solution at a high level using knowledge I previously had attained from debugging Zenoh in the past.

This PR was heavily assisted with the use of AI, specifically the following models:
- `GPT 6.0 astra, medium`, primarily for implementation iterations
- `GPT 5.6 sol, medium`, primarily for questioning the existing implementation at the end and other miscellaneous larger-reasoning inspection
- `GPT 5.6 luna, xhigh`, primarily for investigating the existing code base and spitballing a short-order plan without any real action

### What does this PR do?

Adds an `advertise_addr=<mode>` option to connection parameters for listen locators, which is forwarded through scouting Hello packets, and allows clients that can handle the connection parameter to use the IP address that was observed from Hello receipt in lieu of the IP address that was enumerated by the locator itself.

This does not affect gossip mode enumeration, only direct scouting.

Older zenoh versions **should** (I did not test this case) use the regular scouting IP and ignore the new scouting connection parameter, so this should not be a breaking change.

### Why is this change needed?

For providing a means to use Zenoh peer-to-peer with multicast discovery on NAT-enabled networks with PIM routing, a previous approach was done by implementing a locator address override parameter [here](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/pull/2039).

A precise example is a routing setup where routers NAT the `192.168.0.0/24` subnet to an external address, e.g., `123.45.<router_id>.<last_octet>`.

Zenoh clients behind the router a hello is sent from will see a 192.168.0.x address, and ones outside that router will see a 123.45.y.x address.

Without a special means to handle this case, there is no possible way to leverage zenoh discovery in a peer-to-peer fashion (at least that I am aware of).

### Related Issues

None that I am aware of

data.title: Reclaim the receive buffers of stopped io_uring read tasks
data.body:
Fixes #2774.

When a read task is stopped, the buffers still queued in the kernel for its group are never returned to the pool, so link churn keeps growing the mlocked arena (numbers in the issue).

The group of a stopped task is now retired in two steps: the receive is cancelled and the group is kept until the receive's terminal completion, then a `RemoveBuffers` takes back what the kernel still holds. The buffers are recycled only if the kernel reports the same count we tracked, and the group id is released only then. `ReadTask::stop` returns once that is done.

The receives and the cancel are no longer forced onto io-wq. On a 6.1 PREEMPT_RT board the cancel missed a starting forced-async receive about half the time, leaving it armed forever; issued inline, the receive is polled before the submission returns and the cancel finds it. Let me know if there was a reason for the ASYNC flag.

Also fixes the missing-count accounting after an arena expansion, and hands out the region locked at construction instead of expanding right away.

Tests: a churn test on one Reader (with and without traffic, stops under traffic, buffers held across stops) asserts that VmLck stays flat after the first cycle; it goes from 96 KiB to 3 MiB on main. Unit tests cover the accounting and the receive-liveness bookkeeping. Crate tests, Clippy and rustfmt pass on x86_64 6.8 and aarch64 6.1 (4 KiB and 64 KiB pages).

data.title: io_uring reader keeps the provided buffers of stopped read tasks, locked memory grows with reconnects
data.body:
**Describe the bug**

With the `uring` feature, a process that goes through many link (re)connections keeps growing its mlocked memory. We first saw it on robots after repeated router restarts: every uring-enabled process ends up with one anonymous locked mapping of exactly `1.5 MiB * 2^k`, and a router that had been up for 14 hours held 768 MiB that way.

As far as I can tell the cause is in `zenoh-uring`: when a read task is stopped, `BufferGroup::drop` only frees the group id. The buffers that are still queued in the kernel for that group are never removed (there is no `RemoveBuffers` in the crate) and never get back into the Reader's free pool. Since the transport keeps one `Reader` for its lifetime and creates a task per link, every new link needs fresh buffers, and once the pool is empty each new group grows the arena, which doubles it and mlocks the new region.

Two smaller things make it worse:

- in `provide_batches_to_group`, the expansion branch provides `primary.nbufs` buffers but doesn't subtract them from `count`, so `read_buffer` keeps a stale `buffers_missing` and over-provisions later;
- `BatchArena::new` locks the initial region, but nothing ever hands it out (the recycle queue starts empty), so the first group already expands the arena.

The code is unchanged since io_uring support landed (5dd1a2f76); 1.10.0, 1.10.1 and main behave the same.

**To reproduce**

One `Reader::new(4096, 16)`, then in a loop: connect a loopback TCP socket, `setup_read()` the accepted fd, `stop().await`, close both sockets. No data needs to flow. `VmLck` from `/proc/self/status` after each cycle:

| cycle | 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 24 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VmLck | 96 KiB | 192 | 384 | 768 | 1536 | 3072 | 3072 |

With `Reader::new(65537, 16)`, which is what the transport uses by default, 12 cycles go from 1.5 MiB to 24 MiB. Dropping the Reader frees everything. Sending a few messages per link makes the growth start earlier because of the over-provisioning.

To double check the mechanism I added a diagnostic `RemoveBuffers` at group retirement: the kernel reports 16 buffers still held for every retired group, and the growth stops.

Same numbers on x86_64 6.8 and on aarch64 6.1 with 4 KiB and 64 KiB pages.

**Expected behavior**

Once a task's receive is done and the application has released what it got, its buffers should be usable by the next task, so a fixed number of live links shouldn't need more than a fixed amount of locked memory.

**System info**

- Linux x86_64 6.8, aarch64 6.1.83 and 6.1.158-rt
- Zenoh main (d3757e6c3) and 1.10.0, feature `uring`

data.title: OpenSyn's Shm extension changed encoding between 1.9.0 and 1.10.0 while VERSION and PatchType::CURRENT stayed the same
data.body:
Raising this as a versioning question rather than a bug report, since the right fix is yours to pick. It is not a vulnerability, and there is no split-brain.

## What changed

`transport::open::ext::Shm` is `zextz64!(0x2, false)` in 1.9.0 and `zextzbuf!(0x2, false)` in 1.10.0. `VERSION` is `0x09` in both, and `PatchType::CURRENT` is `1` in both.

Extension dispatch matches on `iext::eid(header)`, which is `header & !FLAG_Z` and therefore keeps the ENC bits, while `ext::Shm::ID` has ENC baked in. Each version consequently sees the other's OPEN `Shm` extension as an unknown non-mandatory extension and skips it. The rest of the `OpenSyn` decodes normally.

## Why it is reachable rather than theoretical

The INIT stage is unchanged between the two releases: `InitSyn { alice_segment }` and `InitAck { alice_challenge, bob_segment }` are identical, and INIT's `Shm` extension is `zextzbuf` in both. A mixed 1.9/1.10 pair therefore negotiates SHM all the way through INIT, both sides allocate and open each other's auth segments, and only then is the OPEN extension dropped.

Both versions' `recv_open_syn` return `Ok(())` when the extension is absent, and the skip is logged at `debug!`, so the visible outcome is shared memory quietly not being used. Neither side can conclude SHM is on by itself, so both settle on off.

## Reproducer

One script, two small crates, no daemon needed:

https://gist.github.com/temporaryfix/0a9c66a733e8c68419417dc0dace7ada

The first two cases are positive controls. If either reports ABSENT then `shared-memory` is disabled somewhere and the cross-version results below mean nothing.

```
[1.10.0] Shm::ID = 0x42   VERSION = 0x09   PatchType::CURRENT = 1
[1.9.0]  Shm::ID = 0x22   VERSION = 0x09   PatchType::CURRENT = 1

1.9.0  encodes -> 1.9.0  decodes   ext_shm = PRESENT   (positive control)
1.10.0 encodes -> 1.10.0 decodes   ext_shm = PRESENT   (positive control)
1.10.0 encodes -> 1.9.0  decodes   decoded OK, ext_shm = ABSENT
1.9.0  encodes -> 1.10.0 decodes   decoded OK, ext_shm = ABSENT
```

The whole difference is one header byte: `0x42` (`ENC_ZBUF | 0x2`) against `0x22` (`ENC_Z64 | 0x2`).

## Where this lives

| what | where |
|---|---|
| `pub type Shm = zextz64!(0x2, false)` | `zenoh-protocol-1.9.0/src/transport/open.rs:111` |
| `pub type Shm = zextzbuf!(0x2, false)` | `zenoh-protocol-1.10.0/src/transport/open.rs:111` |
| INIT's `Shm` is `zextzbuf` in both | `src/transport/init.rs:150` |
| `VERSION = 0x09` in both | `src/lib.rs:31` |
| `PatchType::CURRENT = Self(1)` in both | `src/transport/mod.rs:326` |
| `eid(header) = header & !FLAG_Z`, so ENC is part of the match key | `src/common/extension.rs:68` |
| the `ext::Shm::ID` dispatch arm | `zenoh-codec/src/transport/open.rs:175` |
| unknown and non-mandatory, so skipped with a `debug!` | `zenoh-codec/src/common/extension.rs:33-41` |
| a missing extension returns `Ok(())` | `zenoh-transport-1.9.0/src/unicast/establishment/ext/shm.rs:481` |
| the same in 1.10.0 | `zenoh-transport-1.10.0/src/unicast/establishment/ext/shm/auth.rs:544` |

## The question

What should a decoder do when a known extension id arrives with an unexpected ENC? Today it is indistinguishable from an unknown extension, so any future ENC change on any id degrades silently between peers that have agreed on both `VERSION` and `PatchType::CURRENT`.

If the intended rule is to bump `PatchType::CURRENT` whenever an extension's encoding changes, that seems worth writing down somewhere a later change will run into it.

## Not tested

I have not run two daemons against each other. The reproducer works at the codec level, which is where the dispatch happens. Happy to do the daemon version if that would be more useful.

Written with AI assistance. Every claim above was checked against the sources named and by running the reproducer.

data.title: Remove TCP read interest when io_uring handles RX
data.body:
Fixes #2770.

TCP sockets keep READABLE interest after io_uring takes over RX, causing redundant Tokio reactor wakeups.

Before publishing a universal TCP link, convert its stream to a WRITABLE-only `AsyncFd`. The unsafe hook states the exclusive-access requirement. Reject the new link if conversion fails, while preserving writable notifications and write-half shutdown.

A session-level regression fails on 1.10.0 and current main, and passes with this patch. Tests also cover backpressure and half-close. Injecting a registration failure rejects the second link while the first continues delivering messages.

In two 500-message runs, acceptor `epoll_wait` calls fell from 6,084 and 4,631 to zero, with complete delivery. Linux tests, Clippy and feature-disabled checks pass. Include the TCP unit test in the existing io_uring CI job.

data.title: TCP keeps read interest when io_uring handles RX
data.body:
### Describe the bug

In Zenoh 1.10.0, TCP sockets remain registered with Tokio for READABLE events after io_uring takes over RX. Incoming data keeps waking the accepting runtime even though it has no TCP read task to run.

With 500 messages of 1 MiB, the acceptor made 5,838 `epoll_wait` calls. On current main, two runs produced 6,084 and 4,631 calls; removing READABLE interest reduced both runs to zero during the measured interval. Every run received and checked all 500 messages.

### To reproduce

Copy [the reproducer](https://github.com/BOURBONCASK/zenoh/blob/464e7b1c6bc773d63c1008229c06eb16623de8ac/zenoh/tests/uring_tcp.rs) to `zenoh/tests/uring_tcp.rs` in a `1.10.0` checkout and run:

```sh
cargo test --locked -p zenoh --features uring --test uring_tcp -- --nocapture
```

It exchanges a message over TCP, then fails because the established socket still has EPOLLIN. The same test fails on current main and passes with the fix while retaining EPOLLOUT.

### System info

Linux 6.8, x86_64, Zenoh 1.10.0 and main `b4107719c`. io_uring available, sufficient memlock. The syscall counts exclude warmup and shutdown; they are not a throughput measurement.

data.title: Propagate io_uring reactor startup errors
data.body:
Fixes #2768.

`Reader::new` returns before the RX worker starts. If ring creation or the initial `mlock` fails, the manager still selects io_uring and TCP messages stop arriving.

Wait for the worker to finish ring creation, arena allocation and the first submission before returning success. Startup errors then reach the existing Tokio fallback. Ring creation and submission stay on the same thread for `SINGLE_ISSUER`.

Regression tests cover denied setup, denied enter, low memlock and successful startup. The failure cases fail on 1.10.0 and pass with this patch. Linux crate tests and Clippy pass; the low-memlock pub/sub reproduction also receives messages with the fix.

One open point: the constructor waits without a timeout if the RX blocking pool is full. This PR keeps the existing worker pool.

data.title: io_uring startup errors bypass the Tokio fallback
data.body:
### Describe the bug

In Zenoh 1.10.0, a session can open even when its io_uring RX reactor fails to start. TCP messages then stop arriving instead of falling back to Tokio.

`Reader::new` returns before the worker creates the ring and locks the RX arena. Startup errors stay on the worker, so `TransportManager::build` keeps `Some(Uring)`.

### To reproduce

Build the examples from the `1.10.0` tag:

```sh
cargo build --locked -p zenoh-examples --example z_sub --example z_pub --features zenoh/uring
```

Start the subscriber with a low memlock limit, then the publisher in another terminal:

```sh
(ulimit -l 64; target/debug/examples/z_sub -m peer -l tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 --no-multicast-scouting)
```

```sh
target/debug/examples/z_pub -m peer -e tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 --no-multicast-scouting
```

The subscriber logs `Uring reactor error: Unable to reserve initial 1572880 bytes`, opens the session and declares the subscriber, but receives no messages. The same pair works with sufficient memlock.

Expected: return the startup error to the manager and use Tokio RX.

### System info

Zenoh 1.10.0, Linux 6.8, x86_64. Run without `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, which bypasses the memlock limit. io_uring is otherwise available.

data.title: Query immediately returns zero replies after queryable reconnect
data.body:
### Describe the bug

After a queryable disconnects and reconnects, a newly declared querier can immediately return zero replies.

The configured timeout is 10 seconds, but `recv_async()` fails after only a few milliseconds:

The same query works before the disconnection and shortly after the failed call. During the failure, the router receives the querier interest and returns the current queryable declaration, but never receives the query request.

Here's my network topology to reproduce the issue, it may occur in other contexts:

```text
requester (client) → router → responder (client/queryable)
```

- Multicast scouting disabled
- Explicit router endpoint



### To reproduce

Use https://github.com/bdjellabaldebaran/zenoh-queryable-reconnect-repro

Start the router:

```sh
docker run --rm --network host eclipse/zenoh:1.10.0 -l tcp/0.0.0.0:7447
```

Start the provided responder and requester:

```sh
cargo run -- responder
```

```sh
cargo run -- requester
```

Observed output:

```text
before disconnect: reply=pong ...
immediately after reconnect: ZERO REPLIES ... after a few milliseconds
one second later: reply=pong ...
```

### Expected behavior

The query should reach the router or wait for its configured timeout.

### Actual behavior

It immediately completes with zero replies and never reaches the router.

### Possibly related

- [#2204 — `querier.matching_listener` not working after reconnect](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/issues/2204)
- [#2205 — Fix queryable info update after connection loss](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/pull/2205)
- [#2516 — `session.get()` immediately returns zero replies](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/issues/2516)

### Complete logs

The complete router trace is attached here:

[router-trace.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31836419/router-trace.log)

The relevant interval is `12:58:27`–`12:58:38 UTC`.

### Relevant router logs

The first responder (`e88c3da0`) declares the queryable:

```text
2026-09-04T12:58:27.960880Z DEBUG ... src=south:0:client/e88c3da0:2}:declare_queryable ... expr.mapped=repro/service/rpc
2026-09-04T12:58:27.960893Z DEBUG ... register_queryable ... res=repro/service/rpc
```

The requester (`7423bba6`) sends its first query successfully:

```text
2026-09-04T12:58:29.560622Z DEBUG ... src=south:0:client/7423bba6:3}:send_request ... Route query for res repro/service/rpc
2026-09-04T12:58:29.560702Z TRACE ... dirs=[... dst_face ... e88c3da0 ...]
2026-09-04T12:58:29.560716Z TRACE ... Propagate query to south:0:client/e88c3da0:2
2026-09-04T12:58:29.561572Z TRACE ... Route reply for query south:0:client/7423bba6:3:1
```

The responder disconnects and undeclares the queryable:

```text
2026-09-04T12:58:31.962413Z DEBUG ... src=south:0:client/e88c3da0:2}:undeclare_queryable
2026-09-04T12:58:31.962429Z DEBUG ... unregister_queryable ... return=LastUnregistered { res: repro/service/rpc }
2026-09-04T12:58:31.962616Z TRACE ... Received: TransportMessage { body: Close(...) }
```

A new responder connection (`1ea42db7`) declares the same queryable:

```text
2026-09-04T12:58:33.967210Z DEBUG ... New transport opened ... 1ea42db709faea95662245d1b953d5ae
2026-09-04T12:58:33.968543Z DEBUG ... src=south:0:client/1ea42db7:4}:declare_queryable ... expr.mapped=repro/service/rpc
2026-09-04T12:58:33.968562Z DEBUG ... register_queryable ... res=repro/service/rpc
```

Three seconds later, the requester declares its second querier. The router receives the interest and sends the existing queryable declaration:

```text
2026-09-04T12:58:36.564141Z DEBUG ... src=south:0:client/7423bba6:3}:interest{id=2 mode=CurrentFuture opts={K Q} ...}
2026-09-04T12:58:36.564281Z DEBUG ... send_current_queryables ... dst=south:0:client/7423bba6:3
2026-09-04T12:58:36.564385Z TRACE ... Scheduled ... DeclareQueryable ... for transmission to ... 7423bba6
2026-09-04T12:58:36.564443Z TRACE ... Scheduled ... DeclareFinal ... for transmission to ... 7423bba6
```

No `send_request` is received at this time. The requester reports zero replies immediately.

Exactly one second later, another `get()` using the same querier reaches the router and succeeds:

```text
2026-09-04T12:58:37.565388Z DEBUG ... src=south:0:client/7423bba6:3}:send_request ... Route query for res repro/service/rpc
2026-09-04T12:58:37.565408Z DEBUG ... dst=south:0:client/1ea42db7:4 dst.has_queryable=true
2026-09-04T12:58:37.565447Z TRACE ... Propagate query to south:0:client/1ea42db7:4
2026-09-04T12:58:37.565985Z TRACE ... Route reply for query south:0:client/7423bba6:3:2
```

This shows that the failed `get()` never reached the router, while the querier's interest did. After the routing state was refreshed, the next `get()` on the same querier succeeded.

### System info

- Arch linux 
- Zenoh 1.10.0

data.title: feat: make loading the WebPKI root trust store optional.
data.body:
## Description

### What does this PR do?
Adds  a new configuration parameter "use_public_pki" to control whether the root trust store for TLS and QUIC connections will load the default WebPKI root certs or not.

The value defaults to true, maintaining the behavior in main today.

Full disclosure: Gemini 3.8 Flash was used to provide an initial review of this PR.

To verify the configuration is being loaded correctly, I set up a peer config with a TLS endpoint as the only valid endpoint, and the currently valid TLS parameters set up such that TLS works. I then launched a simple publisher process with logging set to trace and looked for the messages that are logged when the webpki root store is loaded and when the user cert is added. I verified the right logs showed up at the right time with the new parameter missing, the new parameter set to true, and the new parameter set to false.

I then redid the test for QUIC.

### Why is this change needed?
For my project, I would like to use certificates to identify different participants in the network.

Because I control all of the nodes, I don't need or want a public certificate authority to be used. Digicert's opinion on if something is or is not at some some IP is irrelevant. As set up in main, if I turn on TLS, I wind up having to trust the public PKI system, which is just unnecessary. By setting this new parameter to false, my loaded root cert is the only one that is used, which is what I want.

Not loading the public PKI roots also gives me a sort of lazy method of access control. No one without a cert I sign can get access to my system. As set up in main, I would have to also use the other access control methods like passwords on top of just using certs (not that that is a bad idea.)

### Related Issues
Fixes https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/issues/2764

data.title: feat: load known_keys_file into pubkey auth allow-list
data.body:
## What this does

`transport/auth/pubkey/known_keys_file` was already a config option, but it was parsed and then ignored — there was a literal `// @TODO: populate lookup file` — so a configured peer allow-list had no effect.

This wires it up: the file is read in `AuthPubKey::from_config` and its keys are loaded into the authenticator's lookup. It holds one or more PKCS#1 PEM `RSA PUBLIC KEY` blocks (matching the existing `public_key_pem` convention), parsed with the `pem` crate.

Closes #1339.

## Fail-closed on misconfiguration

Rather than silently ending up with an authenticator that restricts nothing, these are now hard errors:

- `known_keys_file` set without a key pair — previously this silently disabled the whole pubkey extension.
- a file that parses to zero keys — previously it collapsed into an empty lookup.
- a PEM block that isn't an RSA public key (e.g. a private key or certificate pasted by mistake) — you now get a clear "expected an RSA public key" error instead of a cryptic decode failure.

The handshake enforcement itself (`recv_init_syn` / `recv_init_ack`) is deliberately left untouched.

## Tests

- `from_config`: keys are loaded, plus each of the misconfiguration errors above.
- An FSM round-trip over the acceptor-side lookup check: an empty allow-list denies, an authorized key is accepted, an unauthorized key is rejected.

## Notes

- Adds `pem` as an optional dependency, gated behind the `auth_pubkey` feature.

data.title: linux abstract socket support + flock migration
data.body: One issue I've had with `transport_unixsock-stream` is stale files surviving process crashes (which happen frequently in my dev environment). I've attempted to fix this by implementing support for Linux abstract sockets and automatically detecting @ prefixes. While adding this feature I discovered a TODO comment noting that flock was deprecated; I made a decision to use the native `std::fs` for file locking which requires [Rust v1.89.0+ (released Aug. 7, 2025)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/fs/struct.File.html#method.lock). data.title: feat(link): add CAN FD multicast and ISO-TP unicast links
data.body:
## Description

### What does this PR do?

Adds two CAN link implementations, both off by default behind new Cargo
features, plus one small extension to the multicast link trait that lets a
medium carry zenoh's QoS onto the wire.

**`transport_can`** -- `zenoh-link-can`, a **multicast** link over a SocketCAN
interface. Endpoint grammar `can/<iface>#bitrate=..;dbitrate=..`. A CAN frame
names a message rather than a destination and every node hears every frame,
which is what a zenoh multicast transport already expects, so a link joins
every other peer on the same bus.

**`transport_isotp`** -- `zenoh-link-isotp`, a **unicast** link over ISO 15765-2.
Endpoint grammar `isotp/<iface>#tx_id=0x..;rx_id=0x..`. The directed identifier
pair is the address. Implemented on the kernel's `CAN_ISOTP` protocol, so
segmentation and flow control happen in-kernel and the link deals in whole
datagrams.

The two share the bus and can run on one peer at once; they are separate link
types because they are separate services.

### Why is this change needed?

CAN is the field bus in vehicles and robots. Reaching a zenoh network from
those nodes means either a gateway box or a link, and this is the link.

The multicast link alone is not enough, which is why both are here. zenoh
routes queries and liveliness tokens to unicast faces only -- `mcast_groups`
appears in the pubsub half of each hat and never in `queries.rs` or `token.rs`.
Over a multicast-only link a peer can publish and subscribe and nothing more,
so anything built on a query silently does not work. ISO-TP supplies a real
unicast face on a bus that has no addresses, and lifts the MTU from one frame
to 4095 bytes as a side effect.

### Design notes worth a reviewer's attention

**CAN FD only, deliberately.** Classic CAN is refused at parse rather than
warned about: a 7-byte payload is smaller than zenoh's per-fragment overhead,
so a classic link cannot make progress at all. It is not a slower link, it is a
non-functional one, and carrying the path would have meant shipping a mode
whose symptom is a hang. (The ISO-TP link has no such limit -- segmentation is
below zenoh there, so classic CAN works fine over it.)

**Priority lives in the frame identifier.** CAN arbitrates by identifier,
lowest wins, so putting zenoh's priority in the high bits makes the bus resolve
collisions in zenoh's favour -- a control message beats a bulk transfer on the
wire rather than behind it. That is the one thing this link can do that a
socket cannot, so it needs the priority of the batch being written.

**Flow control is configurable, because the peer may be small.** The ISO-TP
endpoint takes `stmin` and `bs`, the two knobs ISO 15765-2 gives a receiver:
how long the peer must leave between ConsecutiveFrames, and how many it may
send before waiting for another FlowControl. Left unset the kernel says "send
it all as fast as you like", which is right facing another Linux box and wrong
facing a node with one frame of buffer. Each is one octet of the FlowControl
frame, so a wider value is refused at parse rather than truncated.

**The one trait change.** `LinkMulticastTrait` gains
`write_all_with_priority`, which **defaults to `write_all` and discards the
priority**. No existing link implementation changes. The internal
`send_batch` in `io/zenoh-transport/src/multicast/link.rs` grows a `Priority`
argument to feed it; the transmission pipeline already batches per priority, so
a batch belongs to exactly one and this is not an average over mixed traffic.

### Footprint

29 files, +4657/-16. Two new crates account for nearly all of it; existing
code sees ~105 lines, mostly feature plumbing and enum arms.

The PR is **two commits, one per link**, so the CAN link can be taken and
ISO-TP deferred. The first commit adds no ISO-TP files at all.

### Testing

Tests live in `io/zenoh-transport/tests/{multicast_can,unicast_isotp}.rs` and
run on a virtual bus; `ci/vcan-setup.sh` brings one up.

They are `#[ignore]`-gated because they need a `vcan0` interface, so **CI here
will report them as ignored and effectively test nothing**. Run locally with:

```
sudo ./ci/vcan-setup.sh
cargo test --release --features transport_can,transport_isotp \
  -p zenoh-transport --test multicast_can --test unicast_isotp -- --ignored
```

11/11 pass. Coverage: every DLC boundary, transport-driven fragmentation, a
payload well past one batch, a **four-peer** case (each peer tracks three
remotes told apart only by frame identifier -- a bug in peer-address derivation
is invisible with two peers and obvious with four), priority-major identifier
layout, a datagram larger than one ISO-TP frame, a listener accepting more than
one client in sequence, and **two independent identifier pairs transferring
concurrently** on one bus.

Plus `stmin` and `bs` reaching the wire: 1024 bytes at `stmin=1ms` is about 147
ConsecutiveFrames and cannot complete in under 50ms, where unpaced it takes
12ms. These are kernel state-machine behaviour rather than controller
behaviour, so they are measurable on `vcan` and this is a real test rather than
a simulation.

The concurrency test asserts exact message counts per pair, so a socket
accepting the other pair's frames or a shared reassembly buffer fails it. Verified against a
negative control: pointing both pairs at the same identifiers makes it fail
with `pair 0 received 35 messages, expected exactly 20`. The payload is larger
than one frame, so both transfers segment and interleave; `candump` shows 1510
frames on each pair with 12 FirstFrames and 12 FlowControls.

Also verified interoperating with zenoh-pico over the same bus, and end to end
under ROS 2 via rmw_zenoh -- services, actions, action cancellation, parameters
and graph introspection all cross a CAN bus with no router and no TCP.

**Not covered:** anything about timing or arbitration. `vcan` has no bit rate
and queues frames rather than contending for the bus, so `STmin`, `BS` and the
priority-in-identifier mapping cannot be exercised on a virtual bus. The
concurrency test above shows the addressing and per-socket state are
independent; it says nothing about two peers actually colliding on a wire.

### Companion PRs

- eclipse-zenoh/zenoh-pico#1298 -- the same two links in zenoh-pico. Independent
  of this PR; the two interoperate on one bus but neither needs the other to
  build.
- eclipse-zenoh/zenoh-c#1322 -- forwards the two features to zenoh-c. **Depends
  on this PR** and does not build until it lands.

data.title: fix(runtime): make the connector and listener retry tasks abortable
data.body:
## Description

`TaskController::spawn` documents an obligation on the caller: the spawned task must either run to completion in finite time, or observe the cancellation token from `get_cancellation_token()`. Three spawned tasks do neither, because the work they await is a network connect and they hold no token at all. Three more *do* observe the token, but only around the retry sleep — so they satisfy the contract's letter while still stalling close for `open_timeout`. Both are fixed here; the distinction is drawn below because it decides which sites are urgent.

`Runtime::close_inner` awaits `TaskController::terminate_all_async()` first, and that is:

```rust
self.tracker.close();
self.token.cancel();
self.tracker.wait().await   // unbounded
```

`tracker.wait()` has no timeout of its own — `CloseBuilder`'s 10 s default is the only bound. So a task that never observes the token turns session close into a 10 s stall ending in `"close operation timed out!"`, with nothing naming the cause.

The peer-connector path *does* thread a `CancellationToken` into the task, and `wait_next_peer_retry` correctly `select!`s on it — but only around the retry **sleep**. The blocking connect, `open_transport_unicast(...).await`, is not covered, and runs to `transport.unicast.open_timeout` (10000 ms default). The token is present and used in the one place that is cheap to interrupt, rather than the one that blocks.

### The fix

`spawn` → `spawn_abortable` at six sites. `spawn_abortable` wraps the future in `run_until_cancelled_owned`, so the whole task is dropped at its next await point. The task stays tracked, so shutdown still waits for it; it now yields.

This is the same call already used for the multicast scouting equivalents (`orchestrator.rs:223`, `:343-360`), so it restores consistency rather than introducing a pattern.

| File | Site | Observes the token today? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orchestrator.rs` | `spawn_add_listener` → `add_listener_retry` | **no** — bare `loop`, no token |
| `orchestrator.rs` | `spawn_peer_connector` → `peer_connector_retry` (configured `connect.endpoints`) | yes, but only around the sleep |
| `orchestrator.rs` | `closed_session` → `peers_connector_retry` (reconnect) | yes, but only around the sleep |
| `orchestrator.rs` | `closed_link` → `peer_connector_retry` (reconnect) | yes, but only around the sleep |
| `gossip.rs` | autoconnect → `connect_peer` | **no** — no token check |
| `network.rs` | `connect_discovered_peer` → `connect_peer` | **no** — no token check |

### Two of these are a regression, not a latent bug

- **#2012** ("Fix `Session::close` timeout while client attempts to reconnect", `252f6a883`, 2025-07-24) changed the reconnect path in `closed_session` from `spawn` to `spawn_abortable`, for exactly this reason.
- **#2173** ("Fix multlink reconnect", `225085647`, 2025-10-09) rewrote that function for an unrelated purpose. The `WhatAmI::Client` arm carrying `spawn_abortable` was dropped, and the replacement uses two plain `spawn` calls.

So the close-timeout fix was silently lost in a refactor, and the site count doubled.

### The trigger is narrower than "unreachable peer"

A **refused** connection returns immediately, and the retry sleep that follows is already cancellable — no hang. The hang needs an endpoint that **completes the TCP handshake but not the zenoh handshake**: a paused or frozen container (`podman pause` reproduces it in one command), a firewall that DROPs, or a wedged process.

Close time then tracks `open_timeout` directly, with gossip and multicast both disabled and a single configured endpoint pointed at a `TcpListener` that accepts and sends nothing:

| `open_timeout` | open | close |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10000 ms | 509.95 ms | **9.50 s** |
| 2000 ms | 504.61 ms | **1.50 s** |

It does **not** stack across endpoints — three configured endpoints still cost one `open_timeout`, because the connector tasks overlap.

### Relationship to #2733

#2733 diagnoses the same defect independently and fixes the `gossip.rs` site. That analysis is correct and this PR agrees with it in full — including that `spawn_abortable` is the right remedy rather than a hand-written `select!`.

This PR is offered as the more complete version: the same defect is reachable through four further call sites, including the configured `connect.endpoints` path, which means a deployment that lists peers explicitly and does not use gossip is still affected after #2733. Happy for this to be closed in favour of #2733 plus a follow-up, or for the two to be combined — whichever the maintainers prefer.

Likely also the root cause of **#2675** (`session.close()` blocks ~10 s under bursty packet loss), which has had no comments since July: loss on an *established* link puts you in exactly the completes-TCP-but-not-zenoh case.

### Tests

`zenoh/tests/close_with_failing_listener.rs` is a regression test. It fails without this change (close times out after 10 s) and passes with it — verified both ways.

`zenoh/tests/gossip_timing_probe.rs` is **four `#[ignore]`d diagnostics that assert nothing.** They record how the timings above were measured and are included for the reader rather than for CI. **Suggest dropping this file before merge** — it is deliberately separable, and nothing else depends on it. It is here because reviewers asked for reproducers on similar issues, not because it belongs in the test suite.

### What this PR does not address

`open_transport_unicast` itself remains a bare await. The fix is entirely at the spawn sites, which is minimal and sufficient — but any future `spawn` of that function reintroduces the bug. Worth noting for anyone adding a call site.

data.title: feat(acl): load per-identity access control from a policy store
data.body:
A connected peer's rules can change without restarting the router. The document is fetched at connect, cached, and re-read on PUT @/{zid}/{whatami}/access_control/refresh or when its optional TTL elapses. Fail-closed: refuse the transport when the store cannot be read, and close matching sessions if a refresh fails.

Configured under access_control.policy_store (type redis or postgres); requires --features acl_redis or --features acl_postgres.

## Description

Add an option to load the ACL for a connecting identity from an external store, and to refresh it while the session stays up.

### What does this PR do?

When a transport is admitted and `access_control.policy_store` is set:
- resolve the peer identity from the configured attribute (`username`, `zenoh_id`, or `cert_common_name`)
- fetch the ACL document for that identity from Redis or Postgres
- compile it together with the static `access_control` lists (those lists are then the rules that apply to everyone)
- cache the compiled policy for later interceptors and refreshes

A missing document is not an error: the identity is enforced with the static lists and `default_permission`.
A store that cannot be read is: the transport is refused.
A transport with no such identity attribute is left on the everyone-rules, without a fetch.

Refresh, without a router restart:

- `PUT @/{zid}/{whatami}/access_control/refresh` with the identity as payload (admin space)
- if `entry_ttl_ms` is set (default 300000), a 10s sweep re-reads documents that have gone stale for still-connected identities; `null` disables that and leaves only the explicit PUT

A failed refresh drops the cached policy and closes matching sessions (same fail-closed rule as connect). Ids must not collide between the file and a store document; a collision makes the compiled policy invalid.

Compile-time: `--features acl_redis` and/or `--features acl_postgres`. A config that sets `policy_store` without the matching feature fails at startup. With neither the option nor the feature, behavior is unchanged.

### Why is this change needed?

Static ACL in `config.json5` does not scale to a large, changing fleet: the file grows with every client, and a policy change currently needs a router reload. Fleet management of devices connected to a cloud router is the motivating case: keep only the everyone-rules in the file, and fetch per-identity documents for sessions that are actually connected.

### Related Issues

Related to #1432 and #2659: same motivation (static ACL does not scale for a dynamic fleet). This PR does not implement trust-based / token authorization (#1432) nor key-expression templating (#2659); it adds a router-side per-identity policy store with refresh.

data.title: feat(tls): check full-chain CRLs on mTLS handshake
data.body:
Load PEM/DER CRL files from transport.link.tls.crl and pass them to rustls so leaf and issuer revocation are both enforced.

## Description

Using mtls authentication currently only verifies that the presented certificate is signed by a trusted authority. Some use cases require being able to revoke the ability of a client to connect by presenting a certificate if this certificate has been revoked. A commonly used solution is to distribute CRLs and enforce them at client / server tls connection.

### What does this PR do?

This PR implements certificate revocation check with Certificate Revocation Lists .

It defines a new transport.link.tls.crl option int he config file that can reference one or multiple local files with their filesystem path. 

If one or multiple CRLs are given it expects all certificates in the trust chain (except the trust root) to be validates against a CRL, so e.g. if you use one intermediate certificate authority, you must provide the CRL of the root CA and the CRL of the intermediate CA.

### Why is this change needed?

zenoh does not currently provide any way to take into account certificates revocation.

### Related Issues

None but I can write one if needed, feel free to ask.

data.title: Question and Suggestion: Why is `RingChannelHandler` not `Clone`?
data.body:
Hi Zenoh maintainers,

We are developing [Zenohex](https://github.com/biyooon-ex/zenohex), a Zenoh language binding for Elixir.

Recently, we found an [issue in our binding](https://github.com/biyooon-ex/zenohex/issues/216) in which messages could be lost or delivered out of order during burst traffic. We are currently working to fix this issue, and it is clear that the problem lies in our binding architecture rather than in Zenoh itself.

While reconsidering our receive-side architecture, we noticed that Zenoh provides both `FifoChannel` and `RingChannel`, and we are considering using one of these handlers instead of implementing the corresponding buffering mechanism ourselves.

We have not yet decided which semantics are more appropriate for our architecture:

* `FifoChannel`, which preserves all messages but may block when the channel is full, or
* `RingChannel`, which avoids blocking by dropping the oldest messages when the channel is full.

During this investigation, we noticed one API difference between the two handlers: `FifoChannelHandler<T>` implements `Clone`, while `RingChannelHandler<T>` does not.

Our first question is therefore:

**Is there a design reason why `FifoChannelHandler` is cloneable but `RingChannelHandler` is not?**

Looking at the current implementation, `RingChannelHandler<T>` contains a `Weak<RingChannelInner<T>>`:

```rust
pub struct RingChannelHandler<T> {
    ring: Weak<RingChannelInner<T>>,
}
```

Since `Weak` itself is cloneable, it seems that `RingChannelHandler` could also be made cloneable, for example:

```rust
impl<T> Clone for RingChannelHandler<T> {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        Self {
            ring: self.ring.clone(),
        }
    }
}
```

As far as we can see, this would allow multiple handler instances to refer to the same underlying ring channel without extending the lifetime of `RingChannelInner`.

However, there may be an intended semantic or architectural reason `Clone` is not implemented here, so we would first like to confirm the design with you.

If making `RingChannelHandler` cloneable is considered reasonable and consistent with the Zenoh API design, we would be happy to prepare and submit a PR for this change.

We would appreciate any thoughts or suggestions on this.

data.title: feat: transport link rotation engine
data.body:
## Summary

Implement transport link rotation: a middleware-level capability to automatically close and re-establish transport links on a configurable schedule, enabling cloud-friendly connection cycling.

## Design

- **Make-before-break**: open new link before closing old one — no connectivity gap, no redeclaration storm
- **Fallback to break-before-make**: only if make fails after all retries, as a last resort
- **Interval-only policy**: the RotationPolicy enum has only Interval initially; additional policies can be added later
- **Configurable**: per-endpoint and global, with jitter to avoid synchronized rotation across clients

## Changes

### Config (commons/zenoh-config)
- New `rotation.rs` module with RotationConf, RotationPolicyConf, RotationModeConf, RotationFallbackConf
- Wired into ConnectConfig
- Documented in DEFAULT_CONFIG.json5

### Rotation Engine (zenoh/src/net/runtime/rotation.rs)
- RotationEngine: periodic timer per endpoint, make-before-break with retry+fallback
- Hooked into spawn_peer_connector() in orchestrator

### Transport Layer
- Uses close_link() API from PR #2745 to close individual links

## Configuration Example

```json5
connect: {
  rotation: {
    enabled: true,
    policy: {
      type: "interval",
      interval_ms: 300000,  // 5 minutes
      jitter_ms: 30000,     // ±30s
    },
    mode: "make_before_break",
    fallback: {
      enabled: true,
      max_retries: 3,
      retry_backoff_ms: 1000,
    },
    rotate_across_locators: true,
  }
}
```

## Depends on
- #2745 (transport: add close_link method to TransportUnicast API)

## Investigation Document
Full investigation and design rationale in `docs/transport_rotation_investigation.md`

data.title: fix(zenoh-ext): stop calling user code while holding subscriber state locks
data.body:
## Summary

Two `zenoh-ext` subscribers call user code while they hold a non-reentrant `std::sync::Mutex`. A callback that re-enters the subscriber takes a mutex its own thread already holds. The thread then waits on itself.

This PR records each call under the guard. It replays the call after it releases the guard. `AdvancedSubscriber` and `QueryingSubscriber` both get the fix.

## What changes for a user

| a callback that … | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| undeclares or registers a sample-miss listener | **deadlocks** | works |
| calls `fetch` on a `FetchingSubscriber` | **deadlocks** | works |
| publishes to its own subscriber, conditionally | **deadlocks** | works |
| publishes to its own subscriber on *every* sample | deadlocks | livelocks — still its own recursion (**B5**) |
| panics while another thread stages a call | poisons the mutex, and the subscriber stops working | the subscriber stays usable (**B6**) |

The API does not change. Callbacks still never run concurrently. Samples still arrive in the order the state machine produced them.

## Why it deadlocks

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as Publishing thread
    participant Sub as zenoh-ext subscriber
    participant Core as Session

    App->>Sub: sample arrives
    activate Sub
    Sub->>Sub: zlock!(state)
    Sub->>App: user callback runs, guard held
    App->>Core: publish, fetch, or drop a handle
    Core->>Sub: re-enters on the same thread
    Sub--xSub: zlock!(state) — this thread holds it
    Note over Sub: the thread waits on itself
    deactivate Sub
```

Step 6 takes several shapes. `SampleMissListener::drop` and `SampleMissListenerBuilder::wait` take `statesref`. `FetchingSubscriber::fetch` resolves to `register_handler`, which takes `state`. A callback that publishes re-enters through the session's synchronous local delivery.

The `Drop` shapes reach a user unannounced. A user does not read "drop a value" as "re-enter the middleware".

## The fix

The state walk and the callout interleave, so the callout cannot simply move out of the locked region. Each state gains a FIFO outbox and a `delivering` marker. A thread stages its call under the guard. One thread claims the delivering role and drains the outbox with the guard released.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| state walk | under the guard | under the guard, unchanged |
| the callout | **under the guard** | staged, then called with the guard released |
| delivery order | the guard serialised it | the FIFO preserves it |
| two threads delivering | the guard excluded them | the marker excludes them |
| a callback that re-enters | deadlocks | stages its work and returns |

Each staged call carries the callback handle it is for. An undeclare between the stage and the drain therefore cannot discard the sample.

The two files keep separate copies of this mechanism. `QueryingSubscriber` needs no condition variable. It is also deprecated, so sharing the code would tie a deprecated type's lifetime to the current one's.

## What fails without this

| control | tests | result |
|---|---|---|
| `main`, plus the test file | `AdvancedSubscriber` scenarios | fail: `Got Deadlocked.` |
| commit 1, plus the test file, `querying_subscriber.rs` untouched | 5 reentrancy tests | `3 passed, 2 failed` — the two new ones, both `Deadlocked` |

The second control keeps the first fix and removes only the second. The two new tests therefore pin the second commit.

> [!NOTE]
> Commits 3 to 5 have no failing baseline, and a test cannot honestly give them one. Each closes a race that needs an undeclare, a panic, or a stage to land inside a window bounded by one guard release and the next acquisition. A test that hit such a window would be timing-dependent. A test that missed it would read as proof of absence. The argument for each is the control flow, stated at the code.

## Behaviour changes

| | change | who is affected | action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B1** | `wait_callbacks()` now blocks. It was a no-op | callers who relied on an immediate return | none, unless you depended on the no-op |
| **B2** | callbacks run with the state guard released | callbacks that observed the implicit exclusion | none: exclusion and ordering are preserved |
| **B3** | another thread may deliver your sample | callbacks that read thread-local state | audit callbacks for thread affinity |
| **B4** | the outbox is not backpressure | a producer faster than the callback | none today: the queue grows where the producer used to block |
| **B5** | an unconditional republish livelocks instead of deadlocking | callbacks that publish on every sample | make the republish conditional |
| **B6** | a panicking callback no longer poisons the state mutex | callbacks that panic | none: calls staged during the panic are discarded |

**B3 and B4 are the two to read.** The subscriber never promised a delivering thread, but one thread delivering another thread's sample is new. And the state mutex used to throttle a fast producer as a side effect; nothing bounds the queue now. A bound means dropping samples or restoring a block. Both are larger decisions than removing the deadlock, so this PR does not take them.

## Performance

| added, per delivered sample | note |
|---|---|
| two more uncontended acquisitions of the state mutex | stage, claim the role, then the empty-check that releases it |
| one `Arc` clone and drop | the callback handle each staged call carries |
| a `VecDeque` push, and a drain into the deliverer's buffer | no allocation in steady state: both buffers keep their capacity |
| one `notify_all` with no waiters | a futex check, not a syscall |

That is tens of nanoseconds on a path that has already crossed the network. Contention improves in the case that used to be worst: a slow callback no longer blocks the threads that arrive during it.

Heap residency is one slot per queued call. A slot holds ~280 bytes, because `Call::Sample` is larger than `Call::Miss`. The queue holds about one call while delivery keeps up. Queue depth under a faster producer is **B4**.

> [!NOTE]
> Both readings come from the code. No benchmark was run.

## Testing

`zenoh-ext/tests/reentrancy.rs` adds 5 scenarios. A timeout alone proves nothing, because "the callback ran and wedged" and "the callback never ran" look the same from outside. So:

- Each scenario asserts that it entered the callback.
- `run_scenario` returns `Completed`, `Deadlocked` or `Panicked`. It therefore never reports an assertion failure as a hang.
- `the_callback_guard_fires_when_the_callback_never_runs` is the positive control. It proves the guard executes.
- The scenarios disable scouting, gossip and listeners. They are single-process and need no network.

Full `zenoh-ext` suite: 30 passed, 0 failed. The checks on this page are the current CI state.

This PR adds one `#[allow]`, on the `Call` enum. `clippy::large_enum_variant` wants `Sample` boxed. Boxing it would put a heap allocation on the hot path to shrink a queue that is empty whenever delivery keeps up.

## Breaking changes

None. No public signature, type or name changes.

### Describe the bug

It stuck


### To reproduce

NOTE: we do not have a reliable reproduction -- this is the main thing we need help with.
It appears after hours of production load and we could NOT provoke it synthetically.

1. Run a router under sustained load (~110 sessions, tens of MB/s, SHM enabled).

2. After some hours, new clients stop connecting. Existing sessions are unaffected and
   keep flowing, so the system looks healthy.

3. Confirm the router is wedged -- run this ON THE ROUTER HOST, over loopback:

     import socket
     s = socket.socket(); s.settimeout(3)
     s.connect(("127.0.0.1", 7447))
     s.sendall(b"\x00" * 28)
     try:    s.recv(64); print("ok")
     except socket.timeout: print("WEDGED")

4. Restart with RUST_LOG=zenoh_link_tcp=debug,zenoh_transport::unicast::manager=trace
   and wait for the next occurrence. "Accepted TCP connection" keeps appearing;
   "Accepting link..." stops permanently.

5. Only a zenohd restart recovers it.

Did NOT reproduce it: a local rig with its own router, 30 clients (~88 sessions),
25 hard-killed client processes, malformed handshakes, repeated admin-space queries.

### System info

- Platform: Ubuntu 20.04 64-bit

data.title: Inbound link is never closed when accept_link() returns Err — sockets leak in CLOSE-WAIT
data.body:
### Describe the bug

the Ok(Err(e)) case being discarded, why .is_err() only ever matches Elapsed, that neither arm closes the link, and that the accept_pending branch twelve lines above already does it correctly. Includes the suggested fix and the UnsafeCell aliasing caveat.

 info: version, build flags, rustc, OS, router config, scale.

### To reproduce

1. Start a router with `accept_timeout: 3000` (default config is fine otherwise):
     zenohd -c router.json5

2. Note the baseline on the router host:
     ss -tan | grep ':7447' | grep -c CLOSE-WAIT      # 0

3. Run a client that fails the handshake and then goes away:

     import socket, time
     for _ in range(20):
         s = socket.socket()
         s.connect(("127.0.0.1", 7447))
         s.sendall(b"\x00" * 14)   # half an InitSyn -- decode fails
         time.sleep(5)             # outlast accept_timeout
         s.close()

4. Count again:
     ss -tan | grep ':7447' | grep -c CLOSE-WAIT      # ~20

5. They never clear. Only restarting the router releases them.

data.title: fix: make the gossip autoconnect task abortable
SHM Handoff: growing handoff counter
data.body:
Currently, the SHM size dedicated for handoff counter is fixed and is able to address 351 priority-enabled transport. This is suboptimal from memory-usage perspective and can be not sufficient for some large setups. To address this, an implementation of growing SHM segment for counter is planned.

The growing technique should be taken from `zenoh-uring` memory pool implementation
