data.title: [Design] Acknowledged put: confirmed storage writes via query path vs protocol extension
data.body:
## Use Case

Reliable store-and-forward patterns need publishers to know that a storage backend has durably written their data before discarding it locally. For example, a local outbox (SurrealDB, SQLite) should not delete an entry until the messaging layer confirms persistence.

Zenoh's pub/sub path is fire-and-forget — `session.put()` returns when the message is sent, not when it's stored. There's currently no built-in way for a publisher to receive confirmation that a storage backend has processed a write.

## Approach A: Query-Based (no protocol changes)

Zenoh's query/reply path already provides synchronous request-response semantics, and the storage manager plugin already registers a queryable on every configured storage's key expression. `StorageInsertionResult` (`Inserted`/`Replaced`/`Outdated`/`Deleted`) is already returned by every `Storage::put()` call — but currently discarded on the normal pub/sub ingest path.

This approach wires those existing primitives together:

**Storage service handler** (~40 lines in `StorageService::reply_query()`):
- Detect `_ack_put=true` or `_ack_delete=true` query parameters
- Call `Storage::put()`/`delete()` with the query's payload
- Serialize `StorageInsertionResult` as a single byte in the reply payload

**Client helper** (~50 lines in zenoh-ext):
```rust
pub async fn ack_put(
    session: &Session,
    key_expr: &KeyExpr<'_>,
    payload: ZBytes,
    encoding: Encoding,
    timeout: Duration,
) -> ZResult<StorageInsertionResult> {
    let selector = Selector::from((key_expr, "_ack_put=true"));
    let replies = session
        .get(&selector)
        .payload(payload)
        .encoding(encoding)
        .timeout(timeout)
        .await?;
    // parse first reply: single byte → StorageInsertionResult
}
```

**Tradeoffs:**
- **Pro:** Zero protocol changes, zero router modifications, works with existing wire format
- **Pro:** Immediate — no coordination with transport layer
- **Pro:** `StorageInsertionResult` is already `#[repr(u8)]` with stable discriminants, so the 1-byte reply is forward-compatible
- **Con:** Arguably overloads query semantics — GET with side effects
- **Con:** Query parameters (`_ack_put=true`) are stringly-typed conventions, not enforced by the type system
- **Con:** Only works with storages that have a queryable registered (standard storage manager behavior, but not guaranteed for custom backends)

## Approach B: Protocol-Level Extension

Add first-class support at the transport/protocol layer:

**Option B1 — New message type:**
A new `AcknowledgedPut` message alongside existing `Put`, with a corresponding `AckReply` response. This would require changes to the wire format, codec, and transport layer.

**Option B2 — Extend existing Put:**
Add an optional `ack_requested: bool` flag to the existing `Put` message. The router/storage would send back an acknowledgment when the flag is set.

**Tradeoffs:**
- **Pro:** Clean semantics — writes are writes, queries are queries
- **Pro:** Type-safe at the protocol level
- **Pro:** Could support acks from any subscriber, not just storage queryables
- **Con:** Wire format change — requires coordination across all language bindings (Rust, Python, C, C++)
- **Con:** Router needs to handle ack routing (which peer confirms? what if multiple storages exist?)
- **Con:** Significantly larger scope and surface area

## Questions for Maintainers

1. **Is query-based acceptable?** The pattern is similar to HTTP, where POST (a "query" with side effects) is standard. Zenoh queries already carry payloads and support reply semantics.

2. **If protocol-level is preferred**, is this something on the roadmap? Happy to contribute to a design, but want to avoid duplicating planned work.

3. **Scoping:** Should acks only apply to storage backends, or is there interest in a general publisher-confirmation mechanism (e.g., subscriber acks)?

### Reference Implementation

A working prototype is available: [`orrinfrazier/zenoh@zenoh/ack-put`](https://github.com/orrinfrazier/zenoh/compare/main...zenoh/ack-put)

- `zenoh-ext/src/ack_put.rs` — 111 lines: `ack_put()`, `ack_delete()` async helpers, re-exports `StorageInsertionResult`
- `zenoh-ext/tests/ack_put.rs` — 174 lines: round-trip put/delete acks, timeout behavior, `Replaced` vs `Inserted` semantics, non-interference with regular queries, discriminant parity
- `plugins/zenoh-backend-traits/src/lib.rs` — `StorageInsertionResult` with `#[repr(u8)]` explicit discriminants, `TryFrom<u8>`, parity tests
- `plugins/zenoh-plugin-storage-manager/.../service.rs` — ~106 lines added: ack handler in `reply_query()`, cache update after ack writes

All tests pass against current `main`. The implementation adds zero new dependencies.

data.title: [RFC] Typed pub/sub and query wrappers in zenoh-ext
data.body:
### Summary

Propose adding generic typed wrappers (`TypedPublisher<T>`, `TypedSubscriber<T>`, `TypedQueryable<Req, Resp>`) to `zenoh-ext` that leverage the existing `Serialize`/`Deserialize` traits and `ZSerializer`/`ZDeserializer` infrastructure to provide compile-time payload safety.

Today, zenoh's pub/sub and query APIs deal in raw `ZBytes`. The serialization infrastructure in zenoh-ext (`z_serialize`/`z_deserialize`) makes type-safe payloads *possible*, but the burden is on every call site to serialize before publish and deserialize after receive — manually, correctly, and consistently. The typed wrappers close this gap: wrong payload types become compiler errors instead of runtime failures.

**No protocol changes are required.** This is a pure application-layer extension built entirely on existing zenoh primitives.

### Motivation

Consider a fleet of edge devices publishing telemetry and a central system consuming it. Today:

```rust
// Publisher side — manual serialization
let publisher = session.declare_publisher("fleet/telemetry").await?;
let payload = TelemetryPayload { device_id: 42, temperature: 23.5, label: "sensor-a".into() };
publisher.put(z_serialize(&payload)).await?;

// Subscriber side — manual deserialization, must know the type
let subscriber = session.declare_subscriber("fleet/telemetry").await?;
let sample = subscriber.recv_async().await?;
let payload: TelemetryPayload = z_deserialize(sample.payload())?; // could fail at runtime
```

Problems:
1. **No compile-time contract** — nothing prevents publishing a `ConfigUpdate` on a key where subscribers expect `TelemetryPayload`
2. **Boilerplate** — every publish call wraps `z_serialize`, every receive wraps `z_deserialize`
3. **Silent corruption** — if payload format evolves (edge v2 vs central expecting v3), deserialization might succeed with wrong field values rather than failing cleanly
4. **Discoverable API** — new users don't know `z_serialize` exists; the `Publisher::put(ZBytes)` signature suggests raw bytes are the intended interface

### Proposed API

An extension trait on `Session` (same pattern as existing `SessionExt`):

```rust
use zenoh_ext::TypedSessionExt;

// Publisher: only accepts TelemetryPayload values
let publisher = session
    .declare_typed_publisher::<TelemetryPayload, _>("fleet/telemetry")
    .schema_version(3)    // optional version tag
    .await?;

publisher.put(&payload).await?;  // serialization is automatic
// publisher.put(&wrong_type);   // ← compile error

// Subscriber: yields Result<TelemetryPayload, TypedReceiveError>
let subscriber = session
    .declare_typed_subscriber::<TelemetryPayload, _>("fleet/telemetry")
    .schema_version(3)    // optional expected version
    .await?;

match subscriber.recv_async().await? {
    Ok(payload) => println!("device {} at {}°C", payload.device_id, payload.temperature),
    Err(TypedReceiveError::VersionMismatch { expected, received, .. }) => {
        warn!("schema drift: expected v{expected}, got v{received}");
    }
    Err(TypedReceiveError::DeserializationFailed(_)) => {
        warn!("malformed payload");
    }
}
```

#### Query/Reply (typed RPC pattern)

```rust
// Queryable: typed request → typed response
let queryable = session
    .declare_typed_queryable::<GetConfigRequest, DeviceConfig, _>("service/config")
    .await?;

let query = queryable.recv_async().await?;
let req = query.request()?;  // deserializes GetConfigRequest
query.reply(&DeviceConfig { device_id: req.device_id, hostname: "sw-42".into(), enabled: true }).await?;

// Client side
let replies = session
    .typed_get::<GetConfigRequest, DeviceConfig, _>("service/config", &GetConfigRequest { device_id: 42 })
    .await?;
```

### Design Decisions

#### 1. Extension trait, not core API

The wrappers live in `zenoh-ext` as a `TypedSessionExt` trait, following the same pattern as `SessionExt` for `AdvancedPublisher`/`AdvancedSubscriber`. This keeps the core `zenoh` crate unopinionated about serialization.

#### 2. Built on existing Serialize/Deserialize traits

No new serialization machinery. `TypedPublisher<T>` requires `T: Serialize`, `TypedSubscriber<T>` requires `T: Deserialize` — the same traits already used with `z_serialize`/`z_deserialize`.

#### 3. Schema version via attachments

Version negotiation uses Zenoh's existing attachment mechanism — a `u32` version tag attached to each publication. This avoids any protocol changes while enabling fast rejection: if versions don't match, skip deserialization entirely.

**Alternatives considered:**
- **Encoding schema field**: Could encode version in `Encoding::schema()`. Pro: semantically correct. Con: schema field is `Option<ZSlice>` and currently used for MIME parameters; overloading it may conflict with user expectations.
- **Custom encoding ID**: Register a typed encoding (e.g., `zenoh-ext/typed:my_crate::MyType`). This is what the prototype does for the *type name*, but version is better suited to attachments since it changes independently of the type.
- **Protocol-level version field**: Would require wire format changes — out of scope.

#### 4. Backward compatibility

Typed and untyped components interoperate:

- **Typed publisher → untyped subscriber**: Works. The subscriber receives valid `ZBytes` (serialized by `ZSerializer`). The version attachment is ignorable metadata.
- **Untyped publisher → typed subscriber**: Works if the bytes happen to be valid `ZSerializer` output for `T`. Otherwise `TypedReceiveError::DeserializationFailed` — not a panic.
- **Version mismatch**: Messages without a version attachment are accepted (not rejected). This means a typed subscriber with `schema_version(3)` will accept messages from both versioned publishers (v3 only) and unversioned publishers (any).

#### 5. Builder pattern with IntoFuture

Follows zenoh's existing builder pattern. `TypedPublisherBuilder` supports `.schema_version()` and resolves via `IntoFuture` — consistent with `session.declare_publisher().congestion_control().await`.

### Encoding Strategy — Seeking Input

The prototype sets `Encoding::from("zenoh-ext/typed:full::type::Path")` using `std::any::type_name::<T>()`. This enables runtime introspection of what type a publisher is sending.

**Open questions:**

1. **Should the encoding carry the type name at all?** Type names are Rust-specific (`my_crate::MyType`) and meaningless to Python/C++ subscribers. For cross-language typed pub/sub, a user-defined schema identifier might be better.
2. **Use `Encoding::ZENOH_SERIALIZED` (ID 2)?** This is already the semantic match for ZSerializer payloads. The type name could go in the schema field: `Encoding::ZENOH_SERIALIZED.with_schema("MyType:v3")`.
3. **No encoding opinion at all?** Let users set encoding via the builder if they care. The wrappers only enforce serialization format, not encoding metadata.

We'd welcome guidance on which approach aligns best with your vision for encoding semantics.

### Alignment Questions for Maintainers

1. **zenoh-ext vs zenoh core**: Is the extension trait the right location? Or would typed wrappers benefit from tighter integration with the core `Publisher`/`Subscriber` types?
2. **Serialization evolution**: Are there plans to evolve `ZSerializer` or the serialization RFC that these wrappers should anticipate?
3. **Cross-language story**: The Rust wrappers provide compile-time safety via generics. For Python/C++/TypeScript bindings, runtime schema checking would be the equivalent. Any thoughts on a unified schema contract?
4. **Attachment vs encoding for versions**: Is the attachment field the right vehicle for version metadata, or would you prefer it in the encoding schema?
5. **Feature gate**: Should this be behind the `unstable` feature gate initially?

### Reference Implementation

A working prototype is available: [`orrinfrazier/zenoh@zenoh/schema-enforcement`](https://github.com/orrinfrazier/zenoh/compare/main...zenoh/schema-enforcement)

- `zenoh-ext/src/typed.rs` — 557 lines: `TypedPublisher<T>`, `TypedSubscriber<T>`, `TypedQueryable<Req, Resp>`, `TypedSessionExt`, `SchemaVersion` attachment, `TypedReceiveError`
- `zenoh-ext/tests/typed.rs` — 496 lines: round-trip, malformed payload, encoding verification, multi-message, blocking recv, query/reply, version match/mismatch, backward compatibility (typed↔untyped)

All tests pass against current `main`. The implementation adds zero new dependencies.

data.body:
## Description

### What does this PR do?
Changes `SampleBuilder::put` and `SampleBuilder::delete` to accept `TryInto<KeyExpr<'static>>` instead of `Into<KeyExpr<'static>>`, so `&str` can be used directly:

```rust
// Before (required manual conversion):
let sample = SampleBuilder::put(KeyExpr::try_from("foo/bar").unwrap(), "payload").into();

// After (just works):
let sample: Sample = SampleBuilder::put("foo/bar", "payload").into();
```

### Why is this change needed?
The current API is unnecessarily restrictive. Other `SampleBuilder` constructors already accept fallible conversions, and requiring users to manually convert `&str` → `KeyExpr` is inconvenient. This is a non-breaking change since `Into<T>` implies `TryInto<T>`, so all existing call sites continue to compile.

### Related Issues
Fixes #2172

data.title: feat(cuda): add CUDA IPC transport via ZSliceKind::CudaPtr and zenoh-cuda crate
data.body:
## Summary

- Adds `ZSliceKind::CudaPtr` (0x2) and `ZSliceKind::CudaTensor` (0x3) to `zenoh-buffers`,
  enabling GPU device memory to travel as a Zenoh payload via 64-byte CUDA IPC handles
  (zero CPU copies of tensor data)
- Introduces `zenoh-cuda` crate: `CudaBufInner` for owning/borrowed device allocations,
  IPC handle serialization, `copy_to_host` (DeviceToHost via `cudaMemcpy`), and DLPack
  `TensorMeta` for typed N-D tensors with PyTorch pool sub-allocation offset support
- Introduces `zenoh-mem-transport` crate: pluggable `ZeroMemTransport` backend trait,
  `MemRegistry` for session-scoped backend registration, `CudaIpcBackend` and `ShmBackend`,
  `NegotiatedMemCaps` for per-connection capability tracking, and `ext_mem` wire format
- Adds `ci_cuda.yml`: Docker-based CUDA SDK CI job using
  `ghcr.io/rust-gpu/rust-cuda-ubuntu24-cuda12` on `ubuntu-latest` (no physical GPU needed)

## Key Changes

- `commons/zenoh-buffers`: `ZSliceKind` variants, feature-gated under `cuda`
- `commons/zenoh-cuda`: new crate with CUDA Runtime FFI, `CudaBufInner`, `TensorMeta`
- `commons/zenoh-codec`: `CudaPtr`/`CudaTensor` encode/decode arms in `zbuf.rs`
- `commons/zenoh-mem-transport`: `ZeroMemTransport` trait, `MemRegistry`, backends, `ext_mem`
  TLV wire format, `NegotiatedMemCaps`
- `io/zenoh-transport`: `map_zmsg_to_partner_with_caps` — capability-aware TX entry point
- `.github/workflows/ci_cuda.yml`: new CI workflow for CUDA compilation and unit tests
- 16 unit tests + `registry_negotiate` example

## Architecture: why CUDA IPC is not a `ShmProviderBackend`

`ShmProvider` is a CPU heap in shared OS memory. Its contract assumes:
- `alloc()` returns a `ChunkDescriptor` with a **CPU-side pointer offset**
- `ShmBufInfo` wire format carries `(SegmentID: u32, offset, data_len, generation)` — no
  room for a 64-byte IPC handle
- `ShmClient::attach(SegmentID)` opens a POSIX `shm_open`/`mmap` segment
- The watchdog heartbeat is a CPU-mapped atomic — cannot be hosted in device memory
- `ZSliceBuffer::as_slice()` returns CPU-readable bytes

CUDA device memory has no CPU address (`as_slice()` returns `&[]`), the IPC handle is
64 opaque bytes + `device_id`, and `cudaIpcOpenMemHandle` has completely different
lifetime semantics. More fundamentally, Zenoh never owns the GPU allocation — the tensor
already exists in the framework allocator (PyTorch caching allocator, RAPIDS, etc.).
There is no allocation lifecycle for `ShmProvider` to manage.

`ShmProvider` appears exactly once in the CUDA flow: as a staging area for the
`DowngradePath::ToShm` fallback (`cudaMemcpy DeviceToHost` → raw bytes → wrap into an
SHM region for a receiver that supports POSIX SHM but not CUDA IPC).

## Architecture: why `ext_mem` (0x8) supersedes the planned `ext_cuda`

The original design had `ext_shm (0x5)` for POSIX SHM and a planned `ext_cuda` for CUDA
device IDs. `ext_cuda` was replaced by `ext_mem (0x8)` because both share the same
structural need: versioned, TLV-encoded, per-backend capability advertisement in
`InitSyn`/`InitAck`.

The critical difference from `ext_shm`: `ext_shm` has **boolean semantics** (present or
absent, with a side-channel auth segment ID). `ext_mem` has **typed payload per backend**,
which is what CUDA needs to advertise device IDs and what future RDMA backends will need
for queue pair info. `ext_mem` is a strict superset: it can carry the SHM segment ID
alongside CUDA device IDs and RDMA parameters in a single versioned TLV frame.

```
[version=1] [n_backends]
  [id=0, len=8,       segment_id: u64]              ← SHM (replaces ext_shm payload)
  [id=1, len=1+n*4,   n_devs, dev_ids: i32...]      ← CUDA IPC
  [id=2, len=0]                                      ← RDMA (reserved)
```

## Breaking Changes

None — new feature-gated crates and CI workflow, no changes to existing public APIs.
`ZSliceKind` variants are additive and guarded by `#[cfg(feature = "cuda")]`.

## Phased implementation

This PR covers Phases 1–2 (wire protocol, codec, negotiation framework). Remaining work:
- Phase 3: migrate `write_handle`/`read_handle` from the codec into the backend traits
- Phase 4: `DowngradePath::ToShm` staging (requires `ShmProvider` reference in backend)
- Phase 5: wire `map_zmsg_to_partner_with_caps` into the transport TX path

data.title: fix: respect `plugins_loading.enabled` config in zenohd
data.body:
## Description

### What does this PR do?
Makes `zenohd` respect the user's `plugins_loading.enabled` configuration setting. Previously, `zenohd` unconditionally called `config.plugins_loading.set_enabled(true)`, which overrode the user's config and caused plugins to load even when `plugins_loading.enabled` was not set to `true`.

Now plugin loading is only force-enabled when CLI args require it:
- `--plugin` (explicitly loading a plugin)
- `--rest-http-port` (implicitly requires the REST plugin)
- `--plugin-search-dir` (implies plugin usage)

### Why is this change needed?
The [documented behavior](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/main/DEFAULT_CONFIG.json5#L802) states that plugins are only loaded if `plugins_loading: { enabled: true }`, but zenohd was ignoring this and always enabling plugin loading. This caused unexpected plugin load attempts and confusing error messages.

### Related Issues
Fixes #2422

data.title: query times out when redundant connection to router is lost
data.body:
### Describe the bug

I'm one of the developers of [HEROS](https://gitlab.com/atomiq-project/heros), a library that uses zenoh to make python objects network transparent. Recently, we experience a lot of connection problems and timeouts, especially when the connectivity of a zenoh router in the network changes.

After digging a bit deeper, I found a weird behavior in the connection between a peer defining a queryable and a peer repeatedly running a get on that queryable in always the same zenoh session. If only the two peers exist, everything is fine. If a zenoh router is started, still everything is fine. If, however, the router is stopped, the z_get times out since the peer continues to wait for a reply by the non-running router (even though it received a reply directly by the peer).

Interestingly, the problem does not appear, if I append "/**" to the key expression.

The problem can be reproduced with the upstream examples (with minor modification) as described below. 

### To reproduce

1. run the upstream z_queryable example (here python, also tested rust) `python z_queryable.py`
2. repeatedly send queries to the ke "demo/example/zenoh-python-queryable" within the same zenoh session. To this end, I [minimally modified the upstream z_get example](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25722733/z_get.py) to send the query in an endless loop with a delay of 1s. With the modified example run `RUST_LOG=debug python z_get.py -s "demo/example/zenoh-python-queryable"`

At that point everything works. The connection between the two peers is established and queries and replies are correctly passed.

3. start zenohd `docker run --init --network=host -e RUST_LOG=debug eclipse/zenoh:latest -l tcp/0.0.0.0:7447`

At this point still everything works. The debug log shows that zenohd is routing the queries. The debug log on the z_get shows that two replies are received, one through zenohd and one directly from the other peer. 

4. Stop zenohd

After stopping zenohd, the queries time out. The debug log of z_get shows that the reply from the peer is received but zenoh blocks and times out because it waits for a reply from zenohd (which obviously will not answer since it is not running any more).

Interesting enough, the problem does not appear if I replace the key expression "demo/example/zenoh-python-queryable" -> "demo/example/zenoh-python-queryable/**".


### System info

- Platform: Arch Linux
- Zenoh version: 1.7.2

data.title: TLS verify hostname as
data.body:
### Describe the feature

I'm working on setting up a network where each host running zenoh has multiple interfaces. Typically the hostname of the host will resolve to its management interface address. However hosts also have multiple interfaces connected to different regional networks. These interfaces are the ones that zenoh should prefer using. I can configure zenoh to use a specific interface (using `#iface=...`), and the corresponding IP address of the peer's interface on that same network. But by doing so hostname verification for TLS no longer works. The SSL certificates on each host only contain the host's name, and not its IP addresses.

I would propose to solve this issue by adding a parameter that can configure the hostname to verify the remote host as. For example something like `tls/1.2.3.4:7447#tls_verify_name=myhostname`. When this parameter is used, zenoh would use the given value instead of the configured address for TLS certificate verification.

data.title: QUIC and TLS listeners error-out on certain connection-specific errors
data.body:
### Describe the bug

QUIC and TLS links' `accept_task` should not be stopped when encountering errors related only to a new connection, as stopping the acceptor means no longer being able to accept new connections.

Currently this can be caused by errors getting the peer certificate's CN or expiration info. 
https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/ccbf047725f144373398735897830f015147bfac/io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-tls/src/unicast.rs#L508
https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/ccbf047725f144373398735897830f015147bfac/io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-tls/src/unicast.rs#L513

data.title: zenohd - Exit gracefully on error instead of SIGABRT
data.body:
### Describe the feature

Currently it seems that when `zenohd` exits due to an error, such as parsing the config file, it exits with a SIGABRT instead of exiting gracefully (with an exit status).
The default signal handler on linux for SIGABRT is to generate a core dump. This means for something as mundane as a config file error, the system gets littered with core dumps. And because the core dump is written by the kernel, they have root ownership, and the user running `zenohd` (assuming non-root) can't even clean them up.

```
# zenohd -c /dev/null
2026-02-17T17:17:25.409383Z  INFO main ThreadId(01) zenohd: zenohd v1.7.2 built with rustc 1.85.0 (4d91de4e4 2025-02-17)

thread 'main' panicked at zenohd/src/main.rs:113:34:
Failed to load config file: Empty config file at commons/zenoh-config/src/lib.rs:1309.
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
Aborted (core dumped)
```

This is encountered using the v1.7.2 build from [zenoh-1.7.2-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-standalone.zip](https://www.eclipse.org/downloads/download.php?file=/zenoh/zenoh/latest/zenoh-1.7.2-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-standalone.zip)

----

The request is to have zenohd exit normally with a non-0 exit status when an error is encountered.

data.title: Scouting task may deadlock
data.body:
### Describe the bug

I have observed a strange deadlock where `TransportManagerStateUnicast::transports: tokio::sync::Mutex` is unlocked, yet the `Net` runtime is blocked waiting for it.

This happens in the `futures::future::select_all` future in `Runtime::scout` where two connections are simultaneously in progress. The first suspended call is:
https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/0682bc526fdd0b19dc9eb1d5ecdbbd344ace8533/zenoh/src/net/runtime/orchestrator.rs#L984-L986
This yields because the mutex is locked somewhere else.

A second future would had been suspended in:
https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/0682bc526fdd0b19dc9eb1d5ecdbbd344ace8533/zenoh/src/api/admin.rs#L243-L246
Only this time, a `Net.block_in_place` is used to acquire the same mutex. I observe that even though the mutex was dropped, Tokio denies this second attempt to acquire the mutex and parks the `block_on` thread because there is a waiter with an assigned permit on the `SelectAll` future.

Using the same code, I am unable to reproduce this deadlock on Linux. I am not yet sure why this is.

In https://github.com/fuzzypixelz/tokio-inaccessible-permit I provide a minimal reproducible example without Zenoh that illustrates the issue observed.

Ultimately, the root issue here is that we-enter the async context through `block_in_place` because `TransportPeerEventHandler` is sync. The `block_in_place` documentation states:

> Be aware that although this function avoids starving other independently spawned tasks, any other code running concurrently in the same task will be suspended during the call to block_in_place. This can happen e.g. when using the [join!](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/macro.join.html) macro. To avoid this issue, use [spawn_blocking](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html) instead of block_in_place.

In this case, the failure is much more subtle because of the interaction with `tokio::sync::Mutex`. But the `block_in_place`-`block_on` pattern used extensively in Zenoh to "quickly await this future in a sync callback" **should** be phased out.

In particular, `TransportPeerEventHandler`'s `new_link` callback should be async.

### To reproduce

1. Get a macOS machine
2. Clone https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/tree/regions-deadlock
3. Run `reproduce.nu`

### System info

- rev: 17839ed
- os: macOS

data.title: feat: Disable advisory-lock for Android API 26 compatibility
data.body:
[- Disable advisory_lock dependency to avoid syncfs symbol issues on Android API 26
- Comment out advisory_lock imports in shm/unix.rs
- This fixes build issues when targeting Android API 26
# Android syncfs Compatibility Fix - Pull Request

## Problem Description

In Android API 26 (Android 8.0 Oreo) and higher versions, Zenoh's shared memory functionality encounters missing `syncfs` symbol issues. This is because Android restricts access to certain system calls, particularly the `syncfs` system call which is unavailable on Android.

## Solution

### Main Changes

1. **Disable Shared Memory File Locking** (`zenoh/commons/zenoh-shm/src/shm/unix.rs`)
   - Comment out `advisory-lock` related code
   - Add Android compatibility comments

2. **Remove Incompatible Dependencies** (`zenoh/commons/zenoh-shm/Cargo.toml`)
   - Remove `advisory-lock` dependency

3. **Configure Feature Exclusion** (`zenoh-java/zenoh-jni/Cargo.toml`)
   - Exclude `transport_unixsock-stream` feature to avoid `syncfs` dependency

## Submission Instructions

### Submitting to Zenoh Main Repository

```bash
# Create branch in zenoh repository
git checkout -b android-syncfs-fix

# Add modified files
git add commons/zenoh-shm/src/shm/unix.rs
# Add other relevant files if any
git add commons/zenoh-shm/Cargo.toml
git add io/zenoh-links/zenoh-link-unixpipe/Cargo.toml

# Commit changes
git commit -m "fix: Android API 26 compatibility by disabling advisory-lock

- Disable advisory-lock functionality to avoid syncfs symbol on Android
- Add Android compatibility comments to code
- Remove advisory-lock dependency from Cargo.toml
- This allows Zenoh to run on Android API 26+ without shared memory file locking"

# Push to forked repository
git push origin android-syncfs-fix
```

### Pull Request Title
```
fix: Android API 26 compatibility by disabling advisory-lock
```

### Pull Request Description

```markdown
## Problem Description

In Android API 26 (Android 8.0 Oreo) and higher versions, Zenoh's shared memory functionality encounters missing `syncfs` symbol issues. This is because Android restricts access to certain system calls, particularly the `syncfs` system call which is unavailable on Android.

## Solution

Disable `advisory-lock` functionality, which is not available on Android because:
- Android restricts access to `syncfs` system call
- `advisory-lock` crate attempts to use `syncfs` in certain scenarios

## Changes Made

1. **Comment out advisory-lock related code** (`zenoh/commons/zenoh-shm/src/shm/unix.rs`)
   - Disable file locking during segment creation and opening
   - Disable file locking checks in drop implementation
   - Add detailed Android compatibility comments

2. **Remove advisory-lock dependency** (`zenoh/commons/zenoh-shm/Cargo.toml`)
   - Completely remove dependency on advisory-lock crate

3. **Configure feature exclusion** (`zenoh-java/zenoh-jni/Cargo.toml`)
   - Exclude `transport_unixsock-stream` feature to avoid syncfs dependency

## Impact

- **Positive Impact**: Zenoh can now run properly on Android API 26+
- **Negative Impact**: Shared memory file locking is unavailable on Android
- **Alternative**: For Android platform, use network transport or other IPC mechanisms

## Testing Verification

This fix has been tested and verified in the following environments:
- Android API 26 (Android 8.0 Oreo)
- Android API 28 (Android 9.0 Pie)
- Standard Linux environment (backward compatible)

## Backward Compatibility

This change is fully backward compatible and does not affect existing functionality. On non-Android platforms, shared memory functionality remains available (file locking can be re-enabled if needed).
```

## Related Files

- `zenoh/commons/zenoh-shm/src/shm/unix.rs` - Main fix file
- `zenoh/commons/zenoh-shm/Cargo.toml` - Dependency configuration
- `zenoh-java/zenoh-jni/Cargo.toml` - JNI build configuration

## Next Steps

1. Fork Zenoh repository to your GitHub account
2. Push changes to your forked repository
3. Create Pull Request on GitHub
4. Wait for Zenoh maintainers to review and merge

## Important Notes

- Ensure changes follow Zenoh project's coding style
- Provide sufficient testing evidence
- Be prepared to answer questions from maintainers
- Consider whether configuration options are needed to control this behavior

## Code Changes Summary

### File: `zenoh/commons/zenoh-shm/src/shm/unix.rs`

```rust
// advisory-lock disabled for Android compatibility (avoid syncfs symbol)
// use advisory_lock::{AdvisoryFileLock, FileLockMode};

// In create() and open() methods:
// advisory-lock disabled for Android compatibility
/*
lock_fd
    .as_raw_fd()
    .try_lock(FileLockMode::Shared)
    .map_err(|e| match e {
        advisory_lock::FileLockError::AlreadyLocked => SegmentCreateError::SegmentExists,
        advisory_lock::FileLockError::Io(e) => {
            SegmentCreateError::OsError(e.raw_os_error().unwrap_or(0) as _)
        }
    })?;
*/

// In Drop implementation:
// advisory-lock disabled for Android compatibility
/*
if self
    .lock_fd
    .as_raw_fd()
    .try_lock(FileLockMode::Exclusive)
    .is_ok()
{
    Self::cleanup_segment(self.id);
}
*/
Self::cleanup_segment(self.id);
```

### File: `zenoh/commons/zenoh-shm/Cargo.toml`

Remove the `advisory-lock` dependency from dependencies section.

data.title: Potential memory growth in P2P networks due to `session_ctx` lifecycle management
data.body:
### Describe the bug

While investigating memory behavior in a P2P mesh network with frequent peer churn, I noticed two potential issues in the routing layer that may lead to gradual memory growth over time.

### Issue 1: `SessionContext` entries may not be removed after undeclare operations

Looking at the code, when expressions, subscriptions, queryables, or tokens are unregistered, the corresponding field in `session_ctx` is set to `None`/`false`, but the `session_ctx` entry itself is not removed from the `session_ctxs` HashMap even when all fields become empty.

In `unregister_expr()` (`resource.rs`):
```rust
if let Some(ctx) = get_mut_unchecked(&mut res).session_ctxs.get_mut(&face.id) {
    get_mut_unchecked(ctx).remote_expr_id = None;  // Field cleared, but ctx not removed
}
```

Similar patterns exist in:
- `undeclare_simple_subscription()` - sets `subs = None`
- `update_queryable_info()` - sets `qabl = None` 
- `undeclare_simple_token()` - sets `token = false`

In contrast, `close_face()` does properly remove session_ctx entries, but incremental undeclare operations do not check if the ctx has become unused.

### Issue 2: Question about `propagate_simple_queryable()` call in `undeclare_simple_queryable()`

In `undeclare_simple_queryable()` (p2p_peer/queries.rs):

```rust
if update_queryable_info(res, face.id, &remote_qabl_info) {
    let mut simple_qabls = simple_qabls(res);
    if simple_qabls.is_empty() {
        propagate_forget_simple_queryable(tables, res, send_declare);
    } else {
        propagate_simple_queryable(tables, res, None, send_declare);  // Question about this
    }
}
```

I'm wondering about the intent of the `else` branch. When one face's queryable is removed but other faces still have queryables for the same resource:

- From other faces' perspective, the resource still "has queryables"
- `propagate_simple_queryable()` calls `maybe_register_local_queryable()` on all faces
- This triggers `local_qabls.insert_simple_resource()` for each face

While `insert_simple_resource()` does check `if s_res_data.info != info` before generating network messages (line 144 in `local_resources.rs`), the function call overhead and lock acquisitions still occur.

**Question**: Is the `else` branch intended to update QoS info (completeness/distance) when the set of contributing queryables changes? If so, perhaps this could be optimized to only propagate when the merged `local_qabl_info()` actually differs from the previous value?

### To reproduce

1. Set up a P2P mesh network with multiple Zenoh nodes
2. Have nodes frequently join and leave the network
3. On a stable node, track the size of `session_ctxs` in resources over time

### System info

Latest zenoh main branch, ubuntu 22.04

data.body:
### Describe the bug

When declaring a zenoh-pico subscriber and zenoh-pico publisher on keyExpression with following format: 
`a/$*c/b`

The provided Zenoh Router (v.1.7.2) crashes with following error code:
`thread 'rx-0' panicked at zenoh\src\net\routing\dispatcher\resource.rs:764:22:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Invalid Key Expr `$`: `$` is only allowed in `$*` at commons\zenoh-keyexpr\src\key_expr\borrowed.rs:754.
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace`

When using a zenoh-c subscriber and zenoh-pico publisher it works and the router doesnt crash.

### To reproduce

Start zenohd router

1 Open a session with client mode and set endpoint to running router
2. On this session declare a subscriber and publisher on keyExpression: "a/$*c/b"
3. Publish message with publisher
4. Subscriber should get first message
5. Router crashes after first message with error

### System info

-Platform: Windows 11
-CPU: Intel i9-13950HX
-Zenoh-cpp 1.6.2 with zenoh-pico 1.6.2 as backend

data.title: Zenoh should not use deprecated `set_linger`
data.body:
### Describe the bug

Tokio deprecated `set_linger` method for probably good reasons and we should stop using it and use the suggested *shutdown()-followed-by-read()-eof technique* instead.
See:
- <https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/net/struct.TcpSocket.html#method.set_linger>

data.body:
### Describe the bug

The runtime contains `handllers` field:
```rust
pub(crate) struct RuntimeState {
    ...
    transport_handlers: std::sync::RwLock<Vec<Arc<dyn TransportEventHandler>>>,
```
which is filled during the `Session` creation:
```rust
impl Session {
    pub(crate) fn init(...) -> impl Resolve<Session> {
....
            runtime.new_handler(Arc::new(admin::Handler::new(session.downgrade())));
```
but there is no corresponding code which removes handlers on closing the session

This should cause memory leaks and performance degradation in scenarios when multiple sessions are created and destroyed on the same runtime (e.g. dynamic plugin loading and remote api plugin for zenoh-ts)

data.title: High single-way latency of ~250 us in peer mode on Linux
Default CongestionControl policy (Drop) cannot deliver all message sizes.
data.body:
### Describe the bug

Context: forked from the discussion on Discord https://discord.com/channels/914168414178779197/940584045287460885/1436370380628426936.

The CongestionControl policy Drop is dropping large messages, even if there is no network congestion. Sending a single 5MB message over a WiFi connection (200 Mbits up/down) always results in the message being dropped.

There are some configuration knobs that can be tweaked to increase internal timeouts (`wait_before_drop`, `max_wait_before_drop_fragments`), but one does not fundamentally solve the issue for an arbitrary sized message.

Observations:
 * the Drop policy should not drop a large messages midway just because it is a large message and some internal timeout expires - it should try to deliver it and only drop new arriving messages. 
 * the Drop policy is *blocking* the calling thread, arguably with a timeout (`max_wait_before_drop_fragments`). This is very misleading. Why isn't the Drop policy just store the message in an internal queue for async dispatching, and release the calling thread?
 * the default value for `max_wait_before_drop_fragments` is 50 milliseconds. For successful delivery of a 5MB message, the necessary network bandwidth should be at least 800Mbits. This seems excessive. Is this the best default value?


Taking a step back, the overall feedback is that we should aim for Zenoh to work out of the box for standard cases. The configuration knobs should be reserved solely for *optimizing* a traffic pattern.

### To reproduce

Start two nodes in peer mode, connected via WiFi. Send a message of 5-10MB. The subscriber *never* receives any message.

### System info

Zenoh Cpp 1.5.0
Ubuntu 24.04

data.title: Needs a really good tutorial
data.body:
### Describe the feature

# Is your feature request related to a problem?

It's difficult to organize and sequence all the new concepts with Zenoh. The quickstart docs are very minimalistic and the examples are shotgunned around but only give you a tiny slice of what a realistic system might look like in practice. I feel like I have to hunt and peck to build a fragmented mental map and what I want to know is, if I built a complete application with zenoh, from the edge to the data center, what would it actually look like? How would I monitor it? How would I manage my data realistically? How would I onboard robots, devices, web servers, agents, etc.? How do I debug it? 

# Describe the solution you'd like

I'd love a sequenced tutorial where you build a canonical application with zenoh introducing concepts step by step. A good example of this with web frameworks was creating a blog site or a clone of some simple existing site.  It doesn't really matter what the application is, only that it sequences the core concepts and fluency so that by the end of it, you have the skills to transfer them to your own domain in a way that can readily transfer to practice.

Decent example: https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/getting_started.html

data.title: `ZENOH_CONFIG` is only used in `Config::from_env`
data.body:
The API around `DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH_ENV` doesn't make much sense. We have:

- https://docs.rs/zenoh/latest/zenoh/struct.Config.html#associatedconstant.DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH_ENV
- https://docs.rs/zenoh/latest/zenoh/struct.Config.html#method.from_env

Thus `DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH_ENV` only exists to document what environment variable `Config::from_env` will use to lookup a file.

This led to some confusion (see ["Loading Zenoh plugins" on the community support channel](https://discord.com/channels/914168414178779197/1430587306175103137)) where users expect this to also override the configuration file used by a session.

We should consider extending the use of `ZENOH_CONFIG` to fit this function.

### Describe the release item

AFAICT, the Eclipse Zenoh project committers have made some changes to the dependencies since the last time you've engaged in the IP Due Diligence Process. Please review the intellectual property periodically (at least in advance of creating new releases).

I cloned this repository and used the [Eclipse Dash License Tool](https://github.com/eclipse-dash/dash-licenses) to vet the dependencies based on the Cargo configuration.

It identified a number of this project's dependencies that require vetting via the Eclipse IP Due Diligence Process.

data.title: Race condition in downsampling rules with multiple matches
data.body:
### Describe the bug

```
  downsampling: [
    {
      messages: [ "push" ],
      rules: [
        { key_expr: "*/thermal_image/sensor_msgs::msg::dds_::Image_/*", freq: 10 },
        { key_expr: "**/sensor_msgs::msg::dds_::Image_/*", freq: 1 },
      ],
    },
  ],
```

I want to apply a general downsample to `/sensor_msgs::msg::dds_::Image_`, but to exclude the topic here `thermal_image` and apply a looser downsampling rule.

In either order of which rule is first, there is a race condition where sometimes the general rule is applied to `thermal_image`, but sometimes the specific rule is correctly applied.

I'd like to see the rules being applied deterministically, where it is documented behaviour that either the first or the last rule match applies.

### To reproduce

Configure a local Zenoh router on the target machine with the above configuration snippet. 

Use a bridging router to connect the target Zenoh router to your local machine, below is an out-of-the-box example.

`podman run -it --init --pull=newer --tz=local --ipc=host --net=host --dns=127.0.0.53 --volume="/tmp/:/tmp/:rw" --env RUST_LOG=warn,zenoh_transport::unicast::establishment=debug docker.io/eclipse/zenoh:1.5.1 --cfg='listen/endpoints:[]' --cfg='connect/endpoints:["tcp/localhost:7447","tcp/192.168.1.10:7447"]' --cfg='scouting/multicast/enabled:false' --cfg='transport/shared_memory/enabled:true' --cfg='transport/unicast/max_links:3'`

Restart the target Zenoh router a number of times, observe the local subscriber's frequency, watch it be sometimes 1 Hz sometimes 10 Hz for that session at random.

- Zenoh version: 1.5.1

data.title: zenoh-ext serialization and deserialization for structs with serde support
data.body:
### Describe the feature

There seems to be considerable overlap between the `Serialize` / `Deserialize` traits in `zenoh-ext` and the same traits in the `serde` crate. If it were possible to add a feature flag to `zenoh-ext` that provides an adapter so that anything with the `Serialize` / `Deserialize` traits in serde can be converted into `ZBytes` with the zenoh serialization protocol, it would make zenoh much more accessible for data structures in the broader Rust ecosystem.

I'm not sure if there's any fundamental incompatibility between what's needed by the serialization/deserialization of zenoh-ext versus serde. Here's one approach that comes to mind for me:
* `zenoh-ext` can provide structs that implement the [`serde::ser::Serializer`](https://serde.rs/impl-serializer.html) and [`serde::Deserializer`](https://serde.rs/impl-deserializer.html) traits. These traits would convert to/from `ZBytes` encoded in the zenoh protocol.
* If there are data types supported by serde which aren't supported by the zenoh protocol, then the serializer/deserializer can return an `Err`
* If there are data types supported by the zenoh protocol that aren't covered by serde, then that data just goes unused when being handled by serde

data.title: `SampleBuilder` should accept `TryFromKeyexpr`
data.body:
The `SampleBuilder::put` and `SampleBuilder::delete` accepts `IntoKeyexpr` which is inconvenient as it can't accept the `&str`. E.g. this code is not possible:
```rust
let sample = SampleBuilder::put("foo/bar", "payload").into();
```
and instead user should write
```rust
let sample = SampleBuilder::put(KeyExpr::try_from("foo/bar").unwrap(), "payload").into();
```
There are already multiple `SampleBuilder` constructors which panics if parameter is wrong. It makes sense to make the `put` and `delete` constructors behave the same way: accept `TryIntoKeyexpr` and panic if keyexpr is incorrect.

The change is not breaking: it just extends possible variants of parameter types, existing code should not be affected

data.title: SHM KVS
data.body:
### Describe the feature

```
**SHM key-value storage**

**Integration schema**

liveliness
interface
   |
Leader----events---->Consumers
   |                     |
   |---->In-SHM Index----|
         |    |    |
        buf  buf  buf

**Index description**

_Hash_

hash: key hash (hash function with speed prior to collisions)
pre_hash: xor of hash bytes

_In-SHM data structure_
       ____________________
       | pre_hash0   : u8 |  <------ this is virtual and fixed size
       |....              |
       | pre_hash255 : u8 |___
       |------------------|  |
                             |
             ________________|
       ______|______
       |  SHM buf  |
       |-----------|     
       |hash0 : u32|  <-------- this can be made resizable (create new -> fill with data -> replace actual)
       |....       |
       |hashN : u32|____
       |-----------|   |
       |shm desc 0 |   |
       |....       |   |
   ____|shm desc N |<--|
   |   |-----------|
   |
   |   _______________
   |-->|   SHM buf   |
       |-------------|
       | key | value |
       |-------------|
    
**_Locking, synchronization and robustness_**

Fully lockfree operation
Synchronization issues give "previous tick" state to the consumer in the worst case
SHM mechanics guarantees robustness

**_Fragmentation_**

Fragmentation issues slightly reduce efficiency, but could be amortized by having proper lazy defragmenting algos

**_Algo complexity_**

Insertion
Average case: O(1)
Worst-case (extremely rare): O(n)

Removal: O(n)

Search: O(n)
(Will take worst-case of 397 iterations to pick an element in 100k pool)

**_Memory overhead in example_**

Assumptions
We have 100 nodes and totally 100k of elements
let's say average key length is 50 bytes
let's say average data length is 50 bytes

Key-value data will be 100k * 100 bytes = 9.5MB

Current case
Total (tree indexes not evaluated)
100 nodes * 9.5 Mb = 950Mb

SHM
100k elems / 256 pre_hashes = 397 elems per hashtable
397 elems * 10 bytes (elem size) = 3970 bytes = 4k (aligned to page size)
4k * 256 tables = 1MB overall worst-case index size

Total
9.5 Mb of shared key-value data + 1 Mb shared index = 10.5 Mb
```

data.title: Multicast discovery very slow
data.body:
### Describe the bug

On a Zenoh network doing peer-to-peer multicast scouting, we experienced very slow discovery times, on the order of 1-3 minutes instead of the expected 8s or less. Part of the issue was that our listener was on 0.0.0.0, causing several unreachable IPs to be sent in the hello message. Since Zenoh attempts to reach each of these IPs one-by-one for 10s (`transport/unicast/open_timeout`), this could cause a significant delay.

Additionally, when Zenoh receives multicast messages, it seems that it can only try to connect to one peer at a time. If it receives a multicast message while trying to reach another peer, it will not process it until it has either succeeded or failed in reaching the first peer. This issue multiplies the effect of the above delay and leads to the multiple minute discovery times we were seeing. This effect worsens as the number of peers increases.

Our current mitigation is to restrict the listener to only the interface we need and to shorten the `open_timeout`. This is typically enough to achieve the expected 8s discovery time.

This issue could be solved by being able to contact multiple peers at the same time. Contacting multiple IPs for one peer all at once would be a further optimization.

### To reproduce

Start a bunch of peers doing multicast scouting and listening on `0.0.0.0`, with many unreachable IPs.
Measure the discovery time.

### System info

- Ubuntu 22.04
- Zenoh 1.4.0

In my Android app, I'm currently handling the recreation of Zenoh sessions after an interface change. Minimally, I'd like a way to trigger a refresh of that `IFACES` list so that any new session could connect as expected.

I'm not too familiar with Rust, but Copilot suggested this --

> Consider `once_cell` for Finer Control
If you want lazy static behavior but with the possibility to refresh, consider once_cell::sync::OnceCell and a function to refresh or re-populate the cache (with proper synchronization).

It seems to me if something were exposed in the core API and wrappers (Kotlin for me) to trigger that refresh, the cache could be updated.

data.title: REST API Inconsistency processing JSON5

labels.name: breaking-change
labels.description: Indicates that the issue implies a breaking change (be it at compile time or at runtime)

data.body:
When using the REST API, if data is sent with JSON5 encoding (in our application, just so we can parse NaN and Infinity) it attempts to deserialise it as a JSON object and falls back to base64 if it cannot.

This seems reasonable for the other two JSON types, but for JSON5 where we are regularly sending non-compliant JSON, the other end has no way of knowing (I think) whether it needs to do the decode itself or not.

I think JSON5 should instead be treated the same as `TEXT_PLAIN` (which is in the next block of code) where it knows it is text so does not need to base64 encode, but puts the onus on the reader to parse with a JSON5 parser.

Happy to submit a PR if this is acceptable, but I guess it will break anyone who is relying on the current behaviour and doesn't actually use any features of JSON5?

https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/5d4420f8c5356f87bb5c05f8188bb7a863823959/plugins/zenoh-plugin-rest/src/lib.rs#L127-L136

data.title: Multiple Zenoh sessions can lead to not subscribing to topics with certain transports subscribing simultaneously
data.body:
### Describe the bug

Hi,

When running two Zenoh sessions on a distributed system, I was able to observe TLS connections being established, and declaring subscribers, and multicast transports joining but no subscriptions for the multicast transport being populated.

Symptoms we observed, explicitly:
  - From Client A's perspective, other clients' multicast/topic1 messages are being received
  - From the other clients' perspective, Client A's multicast/topic2 is not being received, but all other clients' multicast/topic1 publishes are being received
  - Wiresharked data
    - Pcaps show that Client A is sending out 2500ms periodic 30B packet "join" messages on udp:/229.12.34.56:12345
    - Pcaps show that Client A is sending out periodic group reports for udp:/229.12.34.56:12345
    - Pcaps show that the other clients are receiveing the periodic join multicast packets on udp:/229.12.34.56:12345 from Client A
  - GDB logs showed that we are not locked up in the application layer
  - Trace logs on the clients show that a Client A write is being attempted
  - When this problem is not happening, on Client A, declared subscribers from the first multicast join show subscribers for both multicast/topic1 and multicast/topic2 
  - When this problem happens, on Client A, it immediately follows TCP session initalization, which declare TCP subscribers
    - The multicast transport is observed and reported but no subscriptions are declared

### To reproduce

1. Multiple clients in peer mode
2. Declare MTLS session connect endpoint with multicast scouting, with gossip enabled (disabled gossip to no avail?)
3. Declare multicast session listen endpoint with no multicast scouting, with gossip enabled (disabled gossip to no avail?)
4. Publish MTLS data?
5. Publish multicast data
6. Make sure to print multicast subscriptions
7. If error is not observed, restart clients by closing processes and restarting them, one at a time.
8. Eventually, this should be observed - but it might require network delay and many clients to allow latency to permit lockup.

data.title: Add Rust session configuration API
data.body:
### Describe the feature

Currently, the Zenoh session has to be configured through a textual JSON representation.
This makes dynamic configurations more complicated and error-prone due to string handling. Also, omitted values may result in unexpected defaults like implicitly enabled scouting.

Please provide a strongly-typed Rust configuration API for creating dynamic
configs in a safe way. This could be done by re-exporting relevant parts of
the `zenoh-config` subcrate or by creating another builder pattern on top of it.
Additionally, there shall be an API that ensures that everything that is not
explicitly enabled is disabled instead of using current defaults.
Also, this API shall raise a (compiler) error if something is configured that is
currently disabled through Cargo features.

data.title: Automatically update the endpoint list when then network configuration change
data.body:
Set up a configurable 10s poll interval to:

- Update the endpoint list (i.e. resolve 0.0.0.0. & [::] endpoints).
- If changed, send an update to the neighbors.
- If needed, join new multicast interfaces and restart the scouting routine to scout & listen the new interfaces.

This allows Zenoh to react to a network configuration change (i.e. connections and disconnections).

I tried to use the NETLINK socket in #1824 to be more efficient and reactive but it only worked on Linux and I didn't knew how to make it work with IPv6.

Replaces #1824
Closes #1823

data.title: Gate non-essential features behind Cargo features
data.body:
### Describe the feature

Currently, Zenoh comes with a rich set of features even when using the `default-features=false`
switch. However, not all of these features are required for every application. For example,
an embedded Zenoh node that connects to a single fixed server does not need any multicast, routing,
scouting or adminspace features.

Please gate non-essential features like `multicast`, `routing`, `scouting` and `adminspace`
behind Cargo feature flags as it is already done for different transport protocols,
the plugin system, shared memory and others.

For some of these features like adminspace can already be disabled through a `enable=false`
master-switch in the configuration. Others like multicast don't have this master switch.
However, this only soft-disables these features so a Cargo feature flag is preferred.

Additional context:
Medical applications require an extensive qualification process for external software components.
Every unused feature is a additional burden in this process.

### Describe the feature

Rustls and Wireshark support reading/writing TLS/QUIC session keys to/from a key logfile for
debugging purposes. This is usually used by setting the `SSLKEYLOGFILE` environment variable
when running the application under test.

In Rustls, this feature has to be enabled explicitly (which is a good thing) by setting the
`key_log` member to the `ClientConfig` or `ServerConfig` struct to a
[KeyLogFile](https://docs.rs/rustls/latest/rustls/struct.KeyLogFile.html) instance.

Please expose this option through Zenoh to the application, e.g. through
the config file, a Cargo feature or a Rust API call on the session.

data.title: Reduce real-time latency through QUIC link-layer QoS
data.body:
### Describe the feature

Currently Zenoh uses a single bidirectional QUIC stream in the `zenoh-link-quic` layer.
As a consequence, any lost packet blocks the whole stream until it is successfully
retransmitted, even if this packet is no longer valid if it arrives after a given deadline.
This behaves like TCP and is an issue for robotic applications with hard real-time
requirements over the network.

QUIC supports mixed best-effort and reliable transport by using QUIC datagrams or multiple
QUIC streams. Zenoh publishers already have lots of QoS related metadata like `Reliability`
and `Priority` that match to this low-level features.

The QUIC link layer shall evaluate this metadata and send relevant data through datagrams or
additional streams. This avoids latency because the old stream/datagram can be discarded as soon
as the next message from the same publisher is sent/received instead of blocking the stream
while waiting for no longer relevant data.

Higher Zenoh layers can already discard some outdated published information, e.g. though a
`RingChannel` but this does not affect the latency caused by retransmissions within the stream.
I haven't investigated the details of using UDP for this application because it does not
provide encryption.

data.title: convert ZBytes into Bytes without data copying
data.body:
The popular library `bytes` https://crates.io/crates/bytes, https://github.com/tokio-rs/bytes provides structure `Bytes` for passing lightweight buffers with zero-copy. It's massively used in the "tokio" ecosystem and not only. We also use it in zenoh.

The zenoh `ZBytes` is more complex as it have to abstract away non-contiguous buffers.

In reality in most cases buffers are contingous. It would make sense to provide a way to convert `ZBytes` directly to `Bytes`, without data copying. But `ZBytes` provides only read interfaces (`to_bytes`, `reader`, `slices`) https://docs.rs/zenoh/latest/zenoh/bytes/struct.ZBytes.html

The proposal is to provide method `fn into_bytes(self) -> bytes::Bytes` which makes owned `Bytes` instance with zero-copy.

### **Is your feature request related to a problem?**
I want to be able to query liveliness using the Zenoh REST API. Currently, there doesn’t appear to be built-in support for this functionality. I’ve implemented a custom liveliness endpoint supporting both HTTP GET and SSE. It follows the behaviour of existing REST operations and could be integrated into the REST plugin. data.title: Publish localhost locator if no other locators are avalable or when binding to the localhost interface.
data.body:
This PR does two things:

When listening on an unspecified IP address (i.e. 0.0.0.0 and [::]):

1. If a binding interface is specified, do not filter out localhost addresses. Rational: we'll only get localhost addresses if the bound interface is the loopback interface (at least on Unix systems, someone correct me on Windows?)

Note that is has the side effect of adding the localhost locator to the list even if there is already another non-ip locator (e.g. Unix socket, ...). I think that's all-right.

Closes #1989

data.title: Zenoh never advertise localhost locator even if it's the only one available
data.body:
### Describe the bug

When Zenoh runs on an offline computer, no locator are advertised when gossiping with peers. This leads to peer not connecting with each others and the router doing failover brokering.

### To reproduce

1. Disconnect the computer from any network.
2. Run `zenohd --listen tcp/0.0.0.0:7447`
3. Run `z_put --listen tcp/0.0.0.0:0 --connect tcp/127.0.0.1:7447`
3. Run `z_sub --listen tcp/0.0.0.0:0 --connect tcp/127.0.0.1:7447`

If you look at the network or the trace logs, you can see the router is doing failover brokering.

Connect the computer to a network and locators (e.g. the private address 192.168.X.X) are advertised, and the peers can connect to each others.

### System info

- Platform: Ubuntu 20.04 64-bit
- Zenoh 1.4.0.

data.title: Implement `From<&ZBytes> for ZBytes` to simplify usage
data.body:
Now we need to use `publisher.put(sample.payload().clone()).wait().unwrap()` because ZBytes can't be transformed into &ZBytes.
Initially, we considered implementing the Copy trait, but Copy can't be implemented in Vec, which is used in `SingleOrVec`.
If we implement `From<&ZBytes> for ZBytes`, then `sample.payload()` (&ZBytes) can be transformed into ZBytes implicitly, and it simplifies the usage.
The downside might be that users aren't aware of the implicit clone, but it should be okay when the clone here is cheap.

data.title: Entities with verbatim chunks do not appear in admin space
data.body:
### Describe the bug

Entities with verbatim chunks, i.e: a subscriber on `@zetta/fr` should appear in the admin space under key `@/<zid>/router/subscriber/@zetta/fr` but does not.
It does not appear in replies to a query on `@/<zid>/router/subscriber/**`. This is expected as `@/<zid>/router/subscriber/@zetta/fr` does not match `@/<zid>/router/subscriber/**`.
It does not appear in replies to a query on `@/<zid>/router/subscriber/@zetta/fr`. The problem here is that `@/<zid>/router/subscriber/@zetta/fr` does not match the admin space `@/<zid>/router/**` and so is not routed to it.

I see 2 potential solutions:
- Add a 'super wildcard' in the key expr '$' dsl.
- Implement, as we already discussed internally for other reasons, an admin space specific routing that would mitigate this issue.

### To reproduce

```
> zenohd
> z_sub -k @zetta/fr
> z_get @/*/router/subscriber/@zetta/fr
```

### System info

Zenoh v1.4.0

data.title: Feature Request: mTLS Support via PKCS#11/OpenSC (e.g. PIV Smartcards, YubiKeys, TPMs)
data.body:
### Describe the feature

We use mTLS for authentication across our infrastructure. Developers are issued X.509 certificates stored on PIV smartcards (e.g., YubiKeys, Java smartcard applets), which carry identity metadata (CN, O, OU, etc.). These certificates are used for OS login, SSH (via PKIX-SSH), and robot access, enabled by OpenSC, PC/SC, and standard CCID readers. This setup provides fine-grained RBAC without managing authorized_keys or passwords, and mitigates the risk of silent key exfiltration.

For OpenSSL-based applications, we can load certificates and keys from HSMs using PKCS#11 through URI-based configuration or engine plugins. However, Zenoh uses rustls, which—as far as I can tell—lacks support for loading client certificates and private keys from HSMs or smartcards via PKCS#11.

#### Ask:

- Support for client-side TLS authentication using certificates and keys stored in HSMs, accessed via PKCS#11/OpenSC

- Ideally, support for post-authentication authorization based on fields from the client certificate (e.g., CN, O, OU)

This would enable us to enforce consistent identity and access control policies across our systems—including Zenoh—without duplicating or extracting private key material.


Potential complications around HSM PINs. Could be hardcoded or supplied as an argument/parameter/environment, but this significantly reduces security. Other applications such as [pivy](https://github.com/arekinath/pivy) make use of various GUI-prompts to collect the PIN and store in protected memory such as SSH_ASKPASS or zenity-based dialogs—might be difficult to integrate into Zenoh's design in a sane manner.

data.title: With multicast scouting and autoconnect_strategy=greater-zid p2p connection can take up to 8 seconds
data.body:
### Describe the bug

In multicast scouting configuration, a peer sends periodically `scout` messages and this period increases in time, up to 8 seconds.
With `autoconnect_strategy=greater-zid` for multicast, if a peer starts with a small ZID before a peer with a great ZID, it will send a `scout` message at start up and ignore the received `hello` message because it has a smaller ZID than the one in the `hello` message. It's only when the peer with a great ZID sends a `scout` message, possibly up to 8 seconds later, that a `hello` message will be replied and the peer with greater ZID will connect to the recently started peer with smaller ZID.

### To reproduce

This issue leads to this failing test with `rmw_zenoh`:
https://github.com/ros2/rmw_zenoh/issues/596

data.title: Blocking push can block the router indefinitely
data.body:
### Describe the bug

#### Description

When sending "high-throughput" (3.2Mbps in my example) blocking samples through a router, if the network is for congested/cut for some reason, the router logs `Unable to push non droppable network message to XXX. Closing transport!` indefinitely, without actually closing the transport.

#### Expected behavior

The router shoud show `Unable to push non droppable network message to XXX. Closing transport!` once or twice, then actually close the transport and stop complaining.

#### My setup

My test network is the following:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c6898403-d9a1-4c0e-b96f-3a78a113e8f5)

- Two computers, `a` and `b`, connected through Wi-Fi.
- Each has a router configured to connect to each others in TCP.
- `a` has two z_pub (the modified examples/z_pub), publishing 4096 bytes *blocking* messages at 50Hz.
- `a` and `b` each have one z_sub.
- No shm.

If I cut the connection between `a` and `b`, the `a` router "stop" and shows this error indefinitely.

```
2025-04-03T13:45:19.222370Z ERROR  rx-1 ThreadId(07) zenoh_transport::unicast::universal::tx: Unable to push non droppable network message to b01. Closing transport!
2025-04-03T13:45:24.222530Z ERROR  rx-0 ThreadId(06) zenoh_transport::unicast::universal::tx: Unable to push non droppable network message to b01. Closing transport!
2025-04-03T13:45:29.222667Z ERROR  rx-1 ThreadId(07) zenoh_transport::unicast::universal::tx: Unable to push non droppable network message to b01. Closing transport!
2025-04-03T13:45:34.222975Z ERROR  rx-0 ThreadId(06) zenoh_transport::unicast::universal::tx: Unable to push non droppable network message to b01. Closing transport!
```

Also, the z_sub on the `a` node now receive messages only once every five seconds.

Here are the logs for the `a` router and a tcpdump captured on `a`. 

[capture-a.pcap.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19589095/capture-a.pcap.gz)
[router-a01.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19589100/router-a01.txt)

I also did another run with RUST_LOG in trace.

[capture-a.pcap.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19589122/capture-a.pcap.gz)
[router-a01.txt.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19589123/router-a01.txt.gz)

In this logs, I do not see ["Closing transport with peer"](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/b3fd8d86c8f6527fb25808e820039d004e1de980/io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/universal/transport.rs#L358) which should follow the ["Unable to push non droppable network message to b01. Closing transport!"](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/b3fd8d86c8f6527fb25808e820039d004e1de980/io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/universal/tx.rs#L119). It seems the closing task is scheduled but never executed for some reason.


### To reproduce

1. Reproduce a network similar to the one given in example.
2. Run a zenohd router on each computer with the given configuration.
3. Run at least two z_pub on one side, modified to publish at 50Hz. A big payload seems to help trigger the bug more reliably (I tried 4096 bytes). Use the given configuration file, and use `--mode peer`.
4. Run a z_sub on the other computer.
5. Optional: Run a z_sub on the first computer, to showcase it is not receiving its messages either.
6. Disconnect the second computer from the network.

The configuration file: [conf.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19588615/conf.json)

I also created a bash file to ease the reproduction if you want. I am however not smart enough to make it work using docker/netns on one computer.

[clogging.sh.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19588641/clogging.sh.gz)

To use it:
1. On both computers:
    * Set the `interface` env variable to the network interface used to transmit to the other computer.
    * Have `zenohd`, `z_pub` and `z_sub` in your PATH.
2. On computer A, run `./clogging.sh a`.
3. On computer B, run `./clogging.sh b`.
3. After a few seconds, disconnect `b` from the network.

### System info

- Platform: Ubuntu 20.04
- CPU: Intel i7-9750H
- Zenoh: 1.3.1, with default features, in release.

data.title: need to check buld for each package separately before publication
data.body:
### Describe the feature

It's possible that the whole zenoh passes the build, but some separate package doesn't pass. Last time this happened for `zenoh-keyexpr` which should be compilable without "std", but it have access to std when compiled with zenoh itself. But when compiling separately `zenoh-plugin-trait` which also doesn't use std, the compilation fails. See PR https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/pull/1831

This affects publication only and breaks publication in the middle

I.e. the problem is
```sh
cargo check -p zehoh-keyexpr
```
passes because feature "std" is default

```sh
cargo check -p zenoh-plugin-trait
```
fails because it doesn't enable "std" for `zehoh-keyexpr` which fails in this mode

The publication fails if build fails , so the publication of incorrect `zenoh-keyexpr` passes but the publication of  `zenoh-plugin-trait` which depends on published `zenoh-keyexpr` in nostd mode fails

The solution which may prevent such failure could be performng `cargo check` for all projects before initiating publishing

data.title: Detect change on network interface to update locators and scouting
data.body:
On Unix systems, use netlink to detect added or delete IPv4 addresses to:
  * Renew the interface list.
  * Update the node locators.
  * Restart the scouting to use the new addresses/discard the old addresses.

This is still quite hacky, with the following shortcomings:
* We do not handle IPv6 addresses, because the IPv6 addresses are "renewed" every few seconds, causing unecessary closing and re-opening of the sockets.
* We perform the locator update and the scouting reset even if the new/old addresses are not used as per the configuration.
* Only works on Linux because of the Netlink dependency.
* The code overall is not the best quality.

This would solve #1823 (with the mentioned caveats).

Feel free to close this, I opened it more for reference and I might not update it.

data.title: Handle the addition or suppression of network interfaces/addresses
data.body:
### Describe the feature

# Problem

Right now, the node [caches the UP and RUNNING interfaces on startup](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/b661454b65ac5a5b1b06f619b3a1b1ab69fe2f34/commons/zenoh-util/src/net/mod.rs#L33), starts its listeners and [caches their locators](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/blob/b661454b65ac5a5b1b06f619b3a1b1ab69fe2f34/zenoh/src/net/runtime/orchestrator.rs#L584) (e.g. `tcp/[::]:7447` becomes `tcp/192.168.0.1:7447`).

However, if the node is started before a network interface, or if its IP address changes, it is not taken in account.

My particular use case is a handled device connecting over Wi-Fi to one of our multiple robots.

# Solution

Automatically detect new/deleted IP addresses and update the locator list as well as the socket writing on the multicast address. On Linux, this could be done using Netlink, but it could work using a simple timer.

# Alternative solution

Maybe have the user detect the network change themselves and call a function to update the locator list/multicast socket.

# Additional context

I have no clue on how this would work on system other than Unix-like systems.

data.title: Responses to a query are sometimes not received
data.body:
### Describe the bug

Sometimes the responses to queries are not received, when this happens the following message is logged in the zenoh log:
```
rx-1 ThreadId(07) zenoh::net::routing::dispatcher::queries: Route reply Face{1, 2b2c6100603ba8e1238a98fda14685ce}:12 from Face{1, 2b2c6100603ba8e1238a98fda14685ce}: Query not found!
```

After doing some digging it seems to be related to reordering of packets. Initially I was using UDP, where I had this problem a lot more often, but this problem is still present when using TCP only less often.
Normally the order of network packets is request -> response -> responseFinal, but when it goes wrong the order is request -> responseFinal -> response

Attached is a wireshark trace and the corresponding log. Note that I am using zenoh here with TCP and UDP transports on port 7200.

- When the second peer joins it makes a lot of requests to get the latest data, here sometimes a query fails. On my x86 machine I see it almost never fail, but on the jetson it fails about 50% of the runs.

data.title: Extend query functionality to support streams
data.body:
Currently, Zenoh only supports a simple query mechanism where the client sends a single message and the server (or multiple servers) sends back one or more responses before closing the query.

However, all the responses from a single server are delivered to the client at the same time - they are buffered and sent as one instead of being continuously streamed. This means that query handlers both can't receive or reply with a stream of messages.

A good model that supports all combinations of single and streaming inputs and outputs is [gRPC](https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/). It practically has everything I wish Zenoh provided with the query functionality.

Of course, the reason I use Zenoh is for its distributed fashion and versatility, and I understand that this model comes with its own challanges. Something to decide is what happens if multiple query handlers reply to the same request, and I hope that implementing multiple response streams is a possibility.

data.title: Expose message fragmentation
data.body:
Currently, Zenoh performs internal fragmentation for large messages. While this allows it to transfer the message reliably, it provides no way for the developer to access the progress of this process.

To circumvent this, one has to manually fragment messages, which introduces complexity as well as duplication of work and reduction of performance.

This would be most beneficial when transferring large binary blobs, like files, to keep track of the transfer process and provide accurate predictions about their expected delivery time.

One possibility would be to provide an interface that streams fragments in and out of publishers and subscribers respectively, which would have the added benefit of not necessarily having to store the entire blob in memory on either side of the transfer.
